note: Every source this archive has opened, whether or not it gave anything up. A search that returns nothing is a result, and the next person should not have to run it again.

rows.src: FindMyPast — National Burial Index, Madeley All Saints
rows.what: William Sneyd of Madeley, the point where this line rests on a web-site citation
rows.got: EIGHT William Sneyds buried at Madeley across 250 years — 1574, 1640, 1659, 1762, 1780, 1791, and TWO that matter: 1819 AGED 88 (born about 1731) and 13 MAY 1827 AGED 84 (born about 1743). The weaver married about April 1769 and was still fathering children in 1794, so neither 1780 nor 1791 can be him. The 1827 burial fits far better — 26 at marriage, 51 at the last child, and within three years of the tree's 1746 — but TWO CANDIDATES ARE TWO CANDIDATES, and the register names no wife, trade or children. The tree gave him no death at all.

rows.what: What became of Charlotte D'Arcy, christened at Chatham eight days before the England sailed
rows.got: CHARLOTTE CATHCART D'ARCY married ROBERT MEAD PEARSON at PARRAMATTA in 1859, registration 2618 — the town where her father George Pitt D'Arcy died in 1849. She would have been 34. The index spells the middle name CATHCART in one entry and CATHERINE in another, and the Chatham baptism gives her no second name at all, so this is a strong candidate rather than an identification. The marriage certificate names the father.

rows.what: A seam this archive has never worked
rows.got: EIGHTY-ONE D'ARCY burials and memorials in Queensland, including Frederick Robert D'Arcy's Toowong transcription which this archive already holds and has already corrected. The other eighty have not been read. Recorded as reachable ground, with the trial expiring; it is an ordinary subscription set and will still be there.

rows.what: Whether the three sisters are buried together — a question this archive had never once searched
rows.got: ALL THREE, ON THE SAME PAGE OF THE SAME REGISTER. ST ANDREW'S OLD CHURCH, Church Road, HOVE, Anglican, page 47: CHARLOTTE died 28 MAY 1869, JANE died 10 JANUARY 1875, CATHERINE died 23 JANUARY 1876. Two exact dates where the archive held only GRO quarters — and Catherine's is the date the Horsham paper printed a fortnight after the event, so a parish register and a newspaper now agree without either having seen the other.

rows.what: Captain Robert D'Arcy of the India Company's Army
rows.got: ROBERT WEST D'ARCY, married at BOMBAY in 1846 — and the middle name is the find. WEST is Lady Catherine Georgiana's family name, so Joseph's son carried his mother's peerage surname to India. The index entry is visible; the transcript is PAYWALLED EVEN ON A PAID TRIAL — “Subscribe to unlock exclusive records”, the same gate as the Royal Artillery officers. Indexed, not read.

rows.what: A control, after two more suspicious zeros
rows.got: Adding `sourcecategory=life events (bmds)` to a search returns ZERO whatever else is asked — D'Arcy births 1817-1825, D'Arcy life events in India, both nothing, while the same searches without it return results. The URL shows the value mangled to `life-events-bmds`. Any null this archive has drawn from a query carrying that filter is worthless.

rows.what: When Lady Catherine died, and where
rows.got: CATHERINE GEORGIANA DARCY, AGED 36, “OF BATH”, buried 22 MARCH 1824 at BOURN, CAMBRIDGESHIRE. The age gives a birth about 1788 and makes her twenty-nine at the Bath marriage of November 1817; the residence is the town she married in; and the date measures the gap between Joseph D'Arcy's two families, since he remarried in November 1830. Her third son Richard was born about 1824, the year she died at thirty-six — an inference, and stated as one.

rows.what: English civil registration for the Brisbane line's English generations
rows.got: OPENS WITHOUT A LOGIN AND RETURNS NOTHING. The search page accepts a POST and answers with the results-page furniture and no result rows, for every query. Control: SMITH BIRTHS IN BRISTOL IN 1840 returns zero, which is impossible — as does Wakefield, whose 1840 Bristol registration this archive already holds at vol 11 p.183. Nothing was searched; no null from it is recorded.

rows.what: The Hornby claim and the Keele graft, put to forum specialists
rows.got: “You are not allowed to search for posts in this forum. Please login below or register.” The forum requires an account to SEARCH, let alone to post. No account was created and no credentials entered. The two questions are drafted and are now errand 47 for somebody with a login.

rows.what: FALCO at ARIENZO, the Italian side of the marriage that joins two archives
rows.got: 26 RECORDS, readable WITHOUT signing in and with no bot check. Falco brides and grooms at Arienzo with both parties named — Loffredo, Abatiello, Di Lucia, Librera, Perrotta — and FALCO GIOVANNA married to CRISCI ANIELLO, Crisci being one of the Falco archive's own surnames. Recorded as reachable ground for that archive rather than imported into this one.

rows.src: Antenati — Portale Antenati, Archivio di Stato di Caserta
rows.what: The Arienzo registers, for the Italian side of the marriage that joins this archive to the Falco one
rows.got: 422 REGISTERS FOR ARIENZO, digitised and free: Matrimoni processetti 63, Matrimoni 62, Nati 59, Morti 57, Diversi 45, from 1809. NOT NAME-INDEXED — a search for FALCO returns nothing and so does RUSSO, the commonest surname in Campania, which is the control proving the index is missing rather than the family. They must be read page by page, and the processetti carry birth extracts and parental consents for both parties. This is the FALCO archive's subject, not this one's; recorded here as reachable ground rather than imported.

rows.src: National Library of Ireland — Catholic Parish Registers
rows.what: The Limerick Atkinson, Cole, Creech, Kent, Bowen and Peevers line
rows.got: STRUCTURALLY OUT OF SCOPE, and worth stating rather than searching. The NLI collection is CATHOLIC ONLY. Paul Cole Atkinson is recorded born at ST MARY'S, LIMERICK — the Church of Ireland cathedral parish — and Atkinson, Cole, Creech, Kent, Bowen and Peevers are Protestant settler names. The same shape as the Wicklow problem on /george-pitt: the records this family needs are the ones this source does not hold.

rows.what: The Creech, Atkinson and Mulcahy lines — errand 14

rows.got: Reachable, and behind Login / Register / Subscribe. Co. Limerick and both Tipperarys are among its counties. A subscription, so an errand rather than a search.

rows.what: The South Leith originals behind Jean Ward's baptism
rows.got: The old-parish-register search area answers ACCESS DENIED without an account. No account was created and no credentials entered. The 1754 baptism and the 1747 marriage are already held here from FamilySearch; what this source would add is the register image.

rows.src: Find a Grave — Centenary Memorial Gardens, Brisbane (cemetery 2483416)
rows.what: The Brisbane graves, from a source this archive had never used
rows.got: THREE D'ARCY MEMORIALS, where the archive had none. KENNETH LINDSAY D'ARCY, 17 Aug 1927 – 3 Mar 2010, aged 82, plot SECRET GARDEN (memorial 286540042). AUDREY DELL D'ARCY, 1 Nov 1929 – 1 Aug 2022, aged 92, Garden of Reflection Section E Site 20 (242573098) — the Audrey “Dell” Murdoch the tree marries to Kenneth at Toowoomba in 1952. And CHRISTINE HILDA D'ARCY-EVANS, 15 Jan 1930 – 10 Aug 2017, Garden of Reflection Section C Site 41 (229072083), a name this archive has never held. The cemetery carries 8,387 memorials at 353 Wacol Station Road.

rows.src: Find a Grave — the location filter
rows.what: A control test, before believing three zeros
rows.got: Searching the surname with `location=Queensland, Australia&locationId=state_2118` returns NO MATCHES for D'Arcy, for Darcy and for Sneyd. It also returns NO MATCHES FOR SMITH, which is impossible — while Darcy searched worldwide returns 10,654. That locationId is not Queensland. Every Find a Grave null taken through it is worthless; searching WITHIN a named cemetery works and is what found the three memorials above.

rows.src: This archive's own places file, through tools/atlas.py
rows.what: The seventeen places with no coordinate
rows.got: THIRTEEN REMAIN, and the approximates fell from 67 to 64. The export carried three kinds of damage that stop a gazetteer: HTML escapes never unescaped (“<Ehrstaedt”), nineteenth-century abbreviation (“Butcombe Som Eng”, “of St Quivox, Ayr, Sctl”), and editorial prose in a place field (“Christened in Berkeley”, “Portsmouth, Hampshire, England or West Indies”). A tidy() step now normalises what is handed to the geocoder and NEVER what is printed — the page still shows the place exactly as recorded. Butcombe, Aller, St Quivox, Ehrstaedt, Portsmouth, Santa Maria a Vico and Dürnau are on the map; Buckwall, Deinschwang, Neuhaus, Himley Hall, “Parish of Elmore” and “?” are not, and will not be guessed at.

rows.src: FindMyPast newspapers — Saint James's Chronicle 23 May 1857; London Evening Standard and Morning Herald 25 June 1862
rows.what: The two Richard D'Arcy deaths in the civil index, chased to their notices
rows.got: Neither is the Richard of Priestlands — but one of them opened a whole family. “At St Helier's, JERSEY, RICHARD, THIRD SON of the late LIEUT. COL. D'ARCY, ROYAL ARTILLERY, and LADY CATHERINE, SISTER OF THE PRESENT EARL DE LA WARR, aged 33.” And five years later: “CAPTAIN ROBERT D'ARCY, late of the INDIA COMPANY'S ARMY, son of the late COLONEL D'ARCY of the ROYAL ARTILLERY and LADY CATHERINE, DAUGHTER OF THE LATE AND SISTER OF THE PRESENT EARL DE LA WARR”, died Bangor 14 June 1862. Joseph D'Arcy had a family by a first wife who was a peer's daughter — the CATHERINE GEORGIANA WEST the tree has always given him, married at Bath in 1817 and never looked at. WEST is the family name of the Earls De La Warr.

rows.src: FindMyPast — England & Wales Deaths 1837-2007, Lymington district
rows.what: Whether Richard D'Arcy of Priestlands died there
rows.got: FIVE D'Arcy deaths ever registered at Lymington: JOSEPH 1848, KATHERINE LUCY ELIZABETH 1863, and three in the twentieth century. No Richard. He is in the house in 1841 and is not in the district's register at all — and no Richard D'Arcy or ARCY appears in the 1851 census anywhere in Britain. The two Richard Darcy deaths in the index for 1836-1856 are Liverpool 1848 and West London 1856, neither with an age.

rows.src: FindMyPast newspapers — Oxford University and City Herald, 1 Nov 1806; Chester Courant, 11 Nov 1806
rows.what: Any contemporary notice of Margarett Maria Isabella D'Arcy's marriage
rows.got: “At Chatham, CAPTAIN J. M. JONES, of the ROYAL DENBIGH MILITIA, to MISS D'ARCY, ELDEST DAUGHTER OF COL. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS.” The Chester Courant adds the church and the officiant — Chatham Church, by the Rev. I. T. Jones. This is the EARLIEST record found anywhere naming Robert D'Arcy's corps, thirty-seven years earlier than the notice this archive announced as the first, and it was in the report of that very marriage. It also fixes Margaret as the ELDEST DAUGHTER of the ten children.

rows.src: FindMyPast newspapers — the London Gazette of 30 June 1818, in five papers
rows.what: Joseph D'Arcy's Persian service, which this archive refused to assert from three letters
rows.got: “The Prince Regent has given permission to LIEUT.-COL. D'ARCY to wear the insignia of the SECOND CLASS OF THE IMPERIAL ORDER OF THE LION AND SUN, conferred on him by the KING OF PERSIA; but not to assume any style, appellation, rank, precedence …” Carried by the London Moderator, Mirror of the Times, Englishman, Johnson's Sunday Monitor and Maidstone Journal within a week. The K.L.S. is a Crown grant in the official gazette, and it dates the Persian service to before mid-1818.

rows.what: The five children Joseph D'Arcy's will left his property to
rows.got: All five, named at last: CATHERINE LUCY JANE (23 Jan 1832), JOHN HYDE (30 May 1833), JOSEPHINE (1836), FRANK HYDE (22 Jun 1839) and JOSEPH WILLIAM (6 Jul 1841) — father JOSEPH, mother KATHERINE LUCY ELIZA, the register calling him “Lt Col RA of MILFORD HOUSE”. And Frank's entry carries four words that open a country: “bn 14 Dec 1838 in MADEIRA”.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Hampshire Burials, Surrey Baptisms, school registers and newspapers
rows.what: What became of Joseph's sons
rows.got: JOHN HYDE went to HARROW and died at Southampton on 28 June 1852, AGED NINETEEN — carried as far as the Catholic Telegraph in Dublin. FRANK HYDE married at Lymington in 1863, died at Worcester on 15 June 1868 AGED TWENTY-NINE, and was brought home to be buried at Pennington. His son FRANK HAMILTON HYDE D'ARCY was baptised at Croydon on 26 November 1868 — five months after his father died — and died at Chelmsford in 1910.

rows.what: Any notice of Jean Ward's death
rows.got: “At Chatham, MRS. D'ARCY, THE WIFE OF MAJOR-GEN. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS.” Jean Ward's death notice — and the EARLIEST record found anywhere that gives Robert D'Arcy his corps, twenty years before the 1843 notice this archive had announced as the first. It also corroborates Connolly's major-generalcy of 1819 from a contemporary source.

rows.src: FindMyPast — the 1851 census IMAGE, HO107/1646 f.357 p.59
rows.what: What the enumerator actually wrote
rows.got: Two transcription errors, read off the page. THE NAME: the enumerator writes “Jane D'Arcy” in a clear hand, apostrophe and all; the index split it into a forename “Jane D” and a surname “Arcy”, which is why no D*ARCY search could ever reach them. THE ADDRESS: he writes “19 Western Cott” against schedule 168 and dittoes down to 22, so the sisters are at 22 WESTERN COTTAGES — a numbered house in a named row, which the index renders as a house name of “Western Cottage” with no street. Schedule 172 holds the three of them and no head; next door at schedule 173 is James Hayward, 61, lodging house keeper.

rows.what: The Sussex sisters by ADDRESS and by HOUSEHOLD rather than by surname
rows.got: ALL THREE, at WESTERN COTTAGE, BRIGHTON — HO107/1646 f.357 p.59 sch.172. JANE D ARCY 55, CATHERINE ARCY 50, CHARLOTTE ARCY 40; all three LODGERS, all UNMARRIED, all “Fund holder”. And the birthplaces: JANE and CATHERINE born BARBADOES, CHARLOTTE born LYME, DORSET. An English census confirming the West Indies posting that rested yesterday on two Caribbean christenings and a family tree.

rows.what: Why four days of surname searches had missed them
rows.got: The surname is indexed as ARCY: the enumerator's D' was read as part of the forename or dropped. No search for a surname beginning D and ending ARCY could reach them. They surfaced from a HOUSEHOLD search — Jane, with a Charlotte in the same house, in Brighton — which returns 119 people, the third of whom is “Jane D Arcy”. This archive's own alias list already carries “arcy” as a form of D'Arcy; the queries put to somebody else's index did not.

rows.what: The sisters in 1861
rows.got: Not found by surname (D*ARCY across Sussex and nationally by year; ARCY across Sussex), by the right street (WESTERN COTTAGES does not exist in the 1861 Brighton index at all), by the widened street (WESTERN* returns 718 people, filtered for all three forenames and read), by Bedford Square in 1861 or 1871, by birthplace in Sussex (33 born Barbadoes, read one by one), by birthplace nationally (25 Janes, 16 Catherines), by household fingerprint (the search that found them in 1851), or at Falmer. A null that has earned the name.

rows.what: Deaths of Robert D'Arcy's three surviving daughters in Sussex
rows.got: All three. CHARLOTTE aged 73, Brighton Q2 1869, vol 2B p.152; JANE aged 87, Brighton Q1 1875, vol 2B p.203; CATHERINE aged 86, Brighton Q1 1876, vol 2B p.164. The ages run back to births of about 1795, 1787 and 1789 against the tree's 1794, 1787 and 1789 — two exact, one a year out. Added to this archive the previous day on the authority of web trees alone, now in the public record.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Horsham, Petworth, Midhurst and Steyning Express, 8 Feb 1876
rows.what: Any notice of Catherine D'Arcy's death
rows.got: “On the 23rd ult., at BEDFORD SQUARE, BRIGHTON, MISS CATHARINE D'ARCY, aged 86.” Confirms the exact date the tree gave without a source, confirms she never married, and gives an address the archive did not have.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Index to Death Duty Registers 1796-1903
rows.what: Whether any of the sisters left an estate
rows.got: CATHERINE D'ARCY of Brighton, grant year 1876, Court of Probate, TNA IR 27/396. The register behind it names executors and legatees — the likeliest document to name this family's English descendants after 1850. Charlotte and Jane produce no entry.

rows.what: The sisters in a household
rows.got: JANE 40, CATHARINE 39 and CHARLOTTE 35 D'ARCY, one household, WESTERN BUILDINGS, BRIGHTON, schedule 1912, HO107/1122 bk8 f.37 p.22, with SARAH HARMER, 20, servant. The ages are eleven to thirteen years light against their real ages of 53, 51 and 46 — stated, not hidden, on the page.

rows.what: The sisters between 1841 and their deaths
rows.got: Not in Brighton in any of the three, and not anywhere in England, Wales or Scotland under a wildcard D*ARCY born 1783–1795. Searched by year alone after discovering that combining year and place breaks the query. A real gap: they are in Brighton in 1841 and dying there from 1869.

rows.src: FindMyPast census search — a control test
rows.what: Whether a zero result meant anything
rows.got: IT DID NOT. Jane Smith, born about 1788, Sussex, 1871 census returns ZERO — impossible. The same search returns 60 by year alone and 136 by place alone. Combining YEAROFBIRTH and KEYWORDSPLACE on a census set silently returns nothing and presents it as a clean negative. Every census null this archive has drawn from a query carrying both is worthless.

rows.src: This archive's own 719 data files and pages — tools/crossread.py
rows.what: Every open question, checked against what this site had already published
rows.got: Six of them were answerable or half-answerable from material already here. Robert and Jean had TEN children on the tree, not the five this site listed. Jane D'Arcy, opened as a question the day before, died at Falmer in Sussex in 1875 aged 88. Three children born in Barbados and one at Lyme Regis bracket the West Indies posting to 1786–1792. Robert has a BROTHER on the tree nobody here had mentioned. Lydia has a birthplace, two parents and a death date. Catherine Cotton has four fields. No subscription and no archive were involved.

rows.what: Martha Wakefield, whom this site said might never have existed
rows.got: MARTHA HURFORD died 23 April 1899 (1899/C/3288) — the tree's date to the day — and the index names her parents as JOHN WAKEFIELD and a HUGHES. MARTHA MILLINGEN, died 1898 (1898/B/30782), is Henry Wakefield's by Catherine Duncan. No Martha Wakefield dies in Queensland at all, 1855–1960, and no Wakefield death names James Wakefield and Hannah Saniger as a Martha's parents — though the index carries Ephraim 1868, Aaron 1896, Zillah 1900, Hiram 1905 and Miriam 1909 correctly. Another man's daughter had been grafted onto this family.

rows.what: Any contemporary notice of Constantine D'Arcy's death at Chatham
rows.got: “After a few weeks illness, THE SON OF COL. D'ARCY, CHIEF ENGINEER OF CHATHAM LINES; his remains were interred with military honours.” It documents the relationship a printed roll of 1898 had only asserted, and it gives Robert D'Arcy a POST — the first record to do so. The Kent Herald used the same phrase of the father in 1827.

rows.what: Constantine D'Arcy's commissions, cited to the Gazette
rows.got: Gentleman Cadet to Second Lieutenant, Corps of Royal Engineers, 1 February 1804 (Gazette 15707 p.690, vice Harding); Second to First Lieutenant, 1 March 1805 (Gazette 15789 p.351, vice Dyson). The second is the SAME PAGE as his father's promotion to Lieutenant-Colonel, which this archive published in July without noticing the son nine lines below.

rows.what: All D'Arcy christenings in the Caribbean
rows.got: Two, both St Michael, Barbados, both to Robert and Jane: CONSTANTINE 18 February 1786 and JANE 17 March 1788. The first was already on /hornby; the second had never been counted as a child of this family. Barbados Births & Baptisms 1637-1891, a larger and separate index of the same island, holds neither.

rows.what: A will for John Saniger of Berkeley, or any Saniger of the direct line
rows.got: Two Saniger-variant entries in 14,195: Abraham Synegar, cardmaker of Dursley, administration 1813/8; John Sanigar, carpenter of Oldbury-on-Severn, will 1822/194. NEITHER IS BERKELEY. Searched under wildcards SAN*, SIN*, SYN*, SWA*, so no spelling can hide inside the result. Control: SMITH returns 277. John Saniger left no proved will in the diocesan court.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Ireland Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage Licence Bonds 1623-1866
rows.what: A marriage licence bond for George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White, Wicklow about 1819
rows.got: No George D'Arcy in the set at all, and none of its six Maria Whites married a D'Arcy. More to the point, the DUBLIN DIOCESE ENTRIES EFFECTIVELY END IN 1741 — sorted by year the latest are one 1813, one 1752, then a wall of 1741. The catalogue's 1866 is the whole set's range, not the diocese's. Betham's abstracts end 1810. Neither collection can hold an 1819 marriage.

rows.what: Whether FindMyPast carries Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills after 1800, or any consular registers
rows.got: PCC holdings are a wills index 1750-1800 and an administrations index 1660-1700, and nothing later. Searching the catalogue for “consular” and for “abroad” returns no record sets at all. Three wills and two Le Havre deaths this archive wants are therefore outside it — which is worth knowing before spending a trial on them rather than after.

rows.src: FindMyPast — England & Wales marriages and newspaper notices, Lymington
rows.what: What became of Joseph D'Arcy's five children
rows.got: FRANK HYDE D'ARCY — the Frank aged two at Priestlands in 1841 — married ANNA MARIA SIMPSON at Lymington on 29 September 1863, daughter of R. Salisbury Simpson, her residence given as Bengal; announced in Thacker's Overland News for India and the Colonies, 3 October 1863. Fifty-two D'Arcy records at Lymington run from 1848 to an electoral roll of 2021.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Index to Death Duty Registers 1796-1903
rows.what: Anything further on Joseph D'Arcy's estate
rows.got: JOSEPH D'ARCY of Lymington, Hampshire, grant year 1848, court “PCC and Country Courts”, TNA IR 27/284. The register behind that index states what the estate was worth and names legatees and executors — a second Kew document, and often a better one than the will.

rows.src: British Newspaper Archive — Morning Herald, 13 February 1843
rows.what: Whether any record calls Robert D'Arcy a father and says which D'Arcy he was
rows.got: One does. “At Havre, MARGARET, wife of MAJOR JONES, DENBIGH MILITIA, and DAUGHTER OF THE LATE MAJOR-GENERAL D'ARCY, R.E.” Major-General, Royal Engineers, late — a description with exactly one referent, and this archive holds his 1778 commission, his 1779 marriage, five gazetted promotions and a funeral at Chatham with military honours. It also confirms from thirty-seven years later the Chatham marriage of 1806 that the parish register gave. Three of Robert's five children are now documented as his: Joseph by baptism, George Pitt by a marriage notice, Margaret by this.

rows.src: British Newspaper Archive — Argus and Caernarvon & Denbigh Herald, 1 April 1843
rows.what: John Maddock Jones of Ruabon
rows.got: “21st, at Ingonville, near Havre, MAJOR MADDOCK JONES, late of the ROYAL DENBIGH MILITIA, and PEN-Y-BRYN, RUABON.” He and Margaret died within weeks of each other in Normandy in the early months of 1843 — she in February, he in March. His will was proved on 24 January 1844 and is at Kew as PROB 11/1991/312, still unopened.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Hampshire civil registration and the British Newspaper Archive
rows.what: Elizabeth Pitt, and what she was to the D'Arcys
rows.got: Still open. Her death was registered at LYMINGTON in 1851, so she stayed in the district after Joseph died in 1848 — she was a member of that household, not a visitor on census night. But no death notice for her survives to state a relationship, and the 1841 census records none. The Pitt question has one more fact around it and no answer.

rows.what: What became of Joseph D'Arcy's widow
rows.got: She stayed. “Mrs. D'Arcy … 5 0” appears in a Lymington public subscription got up by the Mayor, among the local clergy and gentry, four years after her husband's death. She is absent from the 1851 census under every Darcy spelling in Hampshire, which the subscription list shows to be a gap in the index rather than a departure.

rows.what: Joseph D'Arcy's marriage, and Richard Darcy of 1784
rows.got: Neither found. No Joseph D'Arcy marries in Hampshire between 1825 and 1835 though his eldest child was born there in 1832 — he was a serving officer and may have married anywhere. And Richard Darcy, aged 57 at Priestlands in 1841, leaves no other Hampshire record at all: he is a name, an age and an address in his brother's house.

rows.what: Joseph D'Arcy's household
rows.got: Twenty people. JOSEPH DARCY, 61, BORN HAMPSHIRE — corroborating the Portsea baptism of 1780 from sixty-one years later. CATHERINE his wife, 42. RICHARD DARCY, 57, born about 1784, of Joseph's own generation and unknown to this archive. Five children: Catherine 9, John 8, Josephine 6, Frank 2, Joseph an infant. And an ELIZABETH PITT, 55 — in the household of Robert D'Arcy's son, while Robert D'Arcy's other son had carried PITT as a middle name since 1783. Then eleven servants. HO107/393 bk4 f.3 p.1 sch.352.

rows.src: Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages — historical index, searched by DATE rather than by name
rows.what: Every person in this archive with a Queensland death and an exact date — twenty-six of them, from 1856 to 1989
rows.got: Twenty-six of twenty-six found, eighteen of them new. The method is the finding: the two earlier sweeps went surname by surname, which finds a man and loses his wife, because she is registered under the name she died with and not the one this archive files her under. Searching the DEATH DATE ALONE, with no name at all, and then matching on the parents' fields, recovered every married woman the surname sweeps had missed — Maria D'Arcy née White (1856/B/50), Catherine Sneyd née Mulcahy, Jane Atkinson née Creech, Maria Atwell née Rossiter, Catherine Jane Murdoch née Matson, Eliza D'Arcy née Keeling, Mary Ann Blume née O'Brien, Sarah Atwell née Wright, Ida Kathleen Darcy née Atkinson, Ivy Miriam D'Arcy née Sneyd and Barbara Murdoch née Atwell. The best single row is GEORGE LINDESAY D'ARCY, died 13 July 1901, registration 1901/B/1510, whose father is entered as GEORGE PITT D'ARCY — a generation of the direct line named by a document rather than by the tree. Every identification rests on the parent fields agreeing, never on a name and a date; read the list on the register page and the couples chain into one another.

rows.src: Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages — historical index
rows.what: Carminantonio Falco's death, given here as 27 April 1988
rows.got: Nothing — and the null is the point. Queensland registers no death of that name on 27 April 1988. He died on 27 APRIL 1985, registration 1985/3063, which is what both Nudgee Cemetery and the registry say. The wrong year is in this archive for the same reason it was in the Falco archive: both took it from the shared family tree. It is the only one of the twenty-six that did not answer, and it did not answer because the date was wrong.

rows.src: British Newspaper Archive — three papers, February–April 1848
rows.what: Joseph D'Arcy's obituary, and what he did with his life
rows.got: A career nobody in this family knew about. “He commenced his military career at THE TAKING OF ST DOMINGO IN 1793; he served also IN SICILY and at THE TAKING OF WALCHEREN; he was FIVE YEARS IN PERSIA IN THE SERVICE OF PRINCE ABBAS MIRZA, son [of the] King of Persia…” Abbas Mirza was the Qajar crown prince rebuilding the Persian army with British help in the 1810s and 1820s, which is why a separate notice gives Joseph as K.L.S. — Knight of the Royal Order of the Lion and the Sun. The Lady's Newspaper of 8 April adds that he left his property to his wife KATHERINE. Three papers carried the notice and the scan breaks in a different place in each; the text is assembled from all three.

rows.src: British Newspaper Archive — London Evening Standard and Morning Post, February–April 1848
rows.what: What became of Joseph D'Arcy after the Army Lists stop in 1844
rows.got: He died a lieutenant-colonel with a Persian knighthood. “On the 7th inst., at Homestead, Lymington, Hants, LIEUTENANT COLONEL D'ARCY, LATE ROYAL ARTILLERY, K.L.S., in the 69th year of his age.” The Morning Post of 3 April adds: “Lieutenant-Colonel JOSEPH D'ARCY, [late] of the Royal Artillery, formerly of PRIESTLANDS, near Lymington, but late of HOME MEAD, Southampton, who died on the 7th of February, at the age of 69, had EXECUTED HIS WILL IN THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY, 1844, leaving …” — and the digitised text stops there. Death registered Lymington, March quarter 1848, volume 8 page 159. A D'Arcy marrying at Lymington in 1863 is described as “son of the late Colonel D'Arcy, R.A.”

rows.what: The marriage of George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White, County Wicklow, about 1819
rows.got: Not findable, and the reason is 1922. A control — SMITH marrying in County Wicklow 1813–1825 — returns twenty-five results from exactly two collections: Ireland Roman Catholic Parish Marriages and Betham's Genealogical Abstracts. There is NO Church of Ireland marriage register for Wicklow in this index. The same holds across Dublin diocese: seventy D'Arcy marriages 1814–1824 and every one Roman Catholic. An officer of the 39th Foot would have married in the Church of Ireland, and those registers are the ones destroyed in the Public Record Office of Ireland fire of June 1922. One candidate was tested and rejected: a Maria White does marry at BRAY, Co. Wicklow on 13 November 1825, but the groom is THOMAS BARRY and Charlotte D'Arcy was six months old by then.

rows.src: British Newspaper Archive — Salisbury and Winchester Journal, 23 September 1805
rows.what: George Pitt D'Arcy's first marriage, and whose son he was
rows.got: FOUND, and it is the first record in this archive to make him anyone's son. “Lately, Captain GEORGE D'ARCY, [of] the [—] foot, SON [of] LIEUT. COLONEL D'ARCY, [to] MISS LUDLAM, OF GUERNSEY.” The same London report of 16 September ran in the Hampshire Telegraph the same day. ROBERT D'ARCY WAS GAZETTED LIEUTENANT-COLONEL ON 1 MARCH 1805, six months earlier — so the rank in the notice is his, to the month. The scan is damaged and the regiment's number is lost; the notice never gives the father's forename; and no cheap way exists to enumerate every Lieut.-Colonel D'Arcy serving in 1805. A very strong identification, not a proof.

rows.what: Where George Pitt D'Arcy was between the Peninsula and the convict ship
rows.got: IRELAND, with the 39th. The British Press of 6 March 1820 has “a party of the 39th regiment, under the command of Major D'Arcy” going to the assistance of the yeomanry alongside Dominick Browne Esq.; the Weekly Freeman's Journal of 2 February 1822 has “the detachment of the 39th regiment quartered in that town, under the command of Major D'Arcy” near Cork. The right country at nearly the right time for the Wicklow marriage the tree claims.

rows.what: His second marriage, to Maria White in County Wicklow
rows.got: Not found. Eleven articles match D'Arcy and Wicklow in that window and none is a marriage notice for him. The press announced his first marriage promptly in two papers, which makes the silence around the second worth noting rather than explaining away — though a second marriage in Ireland, a captain now a major, is far less likely to reach an English paper.

rows.src: FamilySearch Full-Text Search (free) — England, Gloucestershire, Marriages 1538-1989
rows.what: The Berkeley marriage of John Saniger, about 1797, without waiting for the archives
rows.got: Not surfaced. FamilySearch's full-text search runs handwriting OCR over images that were never indexed, and it does cover Gloucestershire — its collections include Parish Records 1499-1858 and a Marriages set of 444 Berkeley-area hits. Searching that Marriages collection for SANIGER returns three results: a marriage bond of 1767 and two marriage record indexes of 1751-1775. Nothing from 1797. The collection is built from diocesan BONDS and licence indexes, and a labouring family marrying by banns leaves no bond — so this is probably the wrong shelf rather than an absent marriage. The enquiry to Gloucestershire Archives stands.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Australia, Marriages and Queensland Burials
rows.what: Frederick Robert D'Arcy, the surveyor
rows.got: Baptised at Chatham in 1811 to George and Mary, he married in NEW SOUTH WALES in 1834 and is in the Queensland burial registers at TOOWONG in 1875. The half-brother of the Australian children had a whole colonial life this archive had only the first line of.

rows.src: FamilySearch (free) — England Marriages 1538-1973, confirmed on FindMyPast
rows.what: Thomas Saniger's marriage, without paying for Ancestry
rows.got: THOMAS SANIGRE married MARTHA GOLDING at BRISTOL on 24 AUGUST 1828 — the date and place the FamilySearch tree gave without a source, now a record. It was hidden by the spelling SANIGRE, the eighteenth form of this surname and the second in one hour to defeat every search that used the others. The index names no fathers, so the entry that would prove Thomas is John Saniger's son is still unseen.

rows.src: Ancestry.com.au, signed in without a subscription
rows.what: The Berkeley marriage of John Saniger and Lydia, about 1797
rows.got: Visible but masked. Ancestry holds GLOUCESTERSHIRE, ENGLAND, CHURCH OF ENGLAND BAPTISMS, MARRIAGES AND BURIALS 1538-1813 — the collection that would contain a Berkeley marriage of 1797 — and returns John Saniger entries in it. Without a subscription every date, place and spouse renders as xxxx. It also holds FIVE John Saniger entries in GLOUCESTERSHIRE WILLS AND INVENTORIES 1541-1858, and Gloucestershire Land Tax Records 1713-1833, neither of which this archive has ever searched.

rows.src: FamilySearch (free, and signed in) — England Births & Baptisms, confirmed on FindMyPast
rows.what: Hannah Saniger's baptism
rows.got: FOUND. HANNAH SANIGOR, baptised at BERKELEY on 18 AUGUST 1804, father JNO SANIGOR. This archive declared the record missing twice, on two separate days, having established by control test that no index reached it. It was indexed the whole time under SANIGOR — one of the very few spellings this site's own alias list did not carry, and one the subscription site's variant matching also missed. The list has been widened from eleven forms to sixteen. The tree gives her birth as 23 July 1805, eleven months later; there is no second Hannah and no burial between, so the likeliest reading is a slipped year.

rows.what: Hannah's mother, and Thomas Sinegar's marriage
rows.got: Two answers and one warning. The shared tree gives John Saniger a wife LYDIA JONES, 1770–1851, married at Berkeley in 1797 — which would name the Lyddya Sinegar living in Hannah's house in 1841. It also gives THOMAS SANIGER (1808–1881) a marriage to MARTHA GOLDING at Bristol St James on 24 AUGUST 1828, eleven children including a Lydia, a Hannah and two sons named John, and a death at Waterloo Lane, Bristol on 1 October 1881. THE WARNING: John Saniger's profile there carries fourteen sources and every one is a baptism. Neither marriage has a record attached. Both are leads to verify, not facts to publish.

rows.what: The Gloucestershire parish registers FindMyPast does not hold
rows.got: Not used. Ancestry is not signed in on this machine, in either browser, and entering somebody's password is not something this archive will do. FamilySearch was already signed in, is free, and turned out to hold the record anyway.

rows.src: FindMyPast — 1841 census and Bristol parish registers
rows.what: Thomas Sinegar of St Philip and Jacob — Hannah's brother?
rows.got: Very probably. Thomas Saniger was baptised at Berkeley on 3 JULY 1808, son of JOHN — so at the census of 30 March 1851 he is FORTY-TWO, which is exactly the age given for the Thomas Sinegar at 7 Oxford Road who says he was born at BERKLEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE. In 1841 he is at Sion Road, Johns Place, with Martha and four children, one of them a LYDIA aged nine (HO107/378 bk5 f.40 p.26). In 1866 his eldest son James christens a daughter LYDIA at St Philip and Jacob. The tree says Hannah's mother was Lydia, and a Lyddya Sinegar aged seventy was living in Hannah's house in 1841. Three generations of the name, in two households a mile apart.

rows.what: The marriage of Thomas Sinegar and Martha, about 1829
rows.got: Not found, in any spelling, anywhere in Gloucestershire between 1822 and 1838. It is the document that would turn a strong inference into a proved one, because a Gloucestershire marriage entry names the father — as his son's did in 1871.

rows.what: Eliza Wakefield, the eldest daughter
rows.got: Baptised at Bristol 14 OCTOBER 1832, father JAMES WAKEFIELD, mother HANNAH — and BURIED there on 4 MAY 1834, AGED 19 MONTHS. With Ellen, who died at five in 1840, that is two of the three daughters this archive believed had been left behind when the family sailed. Neither was left behind.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Bristol, every record type and spelling
rows.what: Martha Wakefield, born about 1836
rows.got: Nothing. No birth registration, no baptism, no burial for a Martha Wakefield born at Bristol between 1831 and 1842. Her sisters Eliza and Ellen both produce baptisms naming James and Hannah; Martha produces nothing. She is not in the family tree either, which gives the couple only Miriam. She has been named on five pages of this site and on present evidence she entered it from my own earlier work with no record behind her.

rows.what: What became of the Sneyds who stayed
rows.got: They stayed in the same street. JAMES SNEYD, engraver, is at WELL STREET in 1871 aged 53 with his son James A, also an engraver; and at 20 WELL STREET in 1881 aged 63, entered as ENGRAVER (POTTER), with a granddaughter Mary Elizabeth MULLOCK (Sneyd). His father Samuel kept the grocer's shop in the same road in 1851 and was buried from No. 91 in 1855. Sixty years, one street — while his brother Samuel Charles was in Queensland.

rows.what: Jean Ward's parents
rows.got: JOSEPH WARD married MARTH[A] GAIRDEN at SOUTH LEITH on 27 OCTOBER 1747, and the entry names her father: WILLIAM GAIRDEN. Seven years before Jean was christened in the same parish. It confirms the mother's surname in the Scots spelling and adds a further generation — the oldest Scot this archive holds.

rows.what: Catherine Cotton's origins
rows.got: Nothing. Searched across the whole county for a birth between 1733 and 1757: she appears only to marry Thomas Saniger at Berkeley in April 1769, and again in the duplicate index entry for the same event. Two women married into this family within two years of each other — one has now yielded three generations and the other none.

rows.what: Jean Ward's baptism at South Leith
rows.got: Found, with both parents. JEAN WARD, baptised SOUTH LEITH, MIDLOTHIAN, 19 JULY 1754 — father JOSEPH WARD, mother MARTHA GARDEN. This archive has said repeatedly that South Leith is not transcribed and her baptism cannot be reached. It is, and it took one search. The tree gives her birth as 1754; her Chatham burial in 1823 makes it about 1756, which is an ordinary stated-age error. And her eldest son, baptised at Portsea in 1780, was called JOSEPH.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Peninsular War, British Army Officers 1808-1814 (RUSI)
rows.what: George Pitt D'Arcy's war service
rows.got: GEORGE D'ARCY, 39th FOOT, 1808 — the same regiment whose detachment he commanded aboard the convict ship England in 1826, and the rank the Chatham baptism register gives him that March. Sixteen years earlier, and a war this archive did not know he had fought.

rows.src: FindMyPast — British Army Lists, Commission Registers and Officer Promotions
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's career, from primary notices rather than Connolly's 1898 book
rows.got: The whole of it, with Gazette citations. 1778: PRACTITIONER ENGINEER AND SECOND LIEUTENANT, the Corps of Engineers — the earliest record of him this archive holds, a year before he married at Portsea. 8 May 1802: Captain to Major in the Army (Gazette 15478 p.468). 1 March 1805: Brevet Major to Lieutenant-Colonel, vice Nepean (15789 p.351). 4 June 1813: Lieutenant-Colonel to Colonel by Brevet, by the Prince Regent (16737 p.1100). 19 July 1813: Colonel, vice Evelegh (16755 p.1431). Forty-nine years to a major-general's grave.

rows.src: FindMyPast — British Army Royal Artillery Officers 1716-1899, and the Army Lists
rows.what: What became of Joseph D'Arcy after his baptism in 1780
rows.got: He went to the guns, not his father's sappers. Joseph D'Arcy is in the Royal Artillery officers' list from 1795, the Army List of 1798, the commission registers of 1802, 1803 and 1826, the promotions of 1803, 1804 and 1806, and the Army Lists of 1840, 1841, 1843 and 1844 — commissioned at about fifteen and still listed at sixty-four. The transcripts are behind a further paywall even on a trial, so this is a career sketched from an index rather than read.

rows.what: A Robert D'Arcy gazetted Cornet in the 17th Light Dragoons, 1804
rows.got: Discarded, and recorded so it is not found again. He is “Gent”, buying a cornetcy by purchase vice Harris in May 1804 — while this family's Robert D'Arcy had been a major since 1802 and was a lieutenant-colonel by the following March. Same name, different man.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Berkeley St Mary the Virgin
rows.what: The two generations above Thomas Saniger of 1744
rows.got: Both found, and both match the tree to the day. THOMAS SANIGER baptised at Berkeley 12 DECEMBER 1711, father WILLIAM — the tree gives his birth as 11 December 1711. WILLIAM SANIGER baptised at Berkeley 12 OCTOBER 1679, father WILLIAM — the tree gives 12 October 1679. That makes six generations of this line on parish record, three of them matching the tree's dates exactly across a hundred and thirty years.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Berkeley St Mary the Virgin
rows.what: Catherine Cotton's origins
rows.got: No baptism for her at Berkeley. She appears in the parish only to marry Thomas Saniger there on 10 April 1769, and where she came from is the one new question this work has opened rather than closed.

rows.what: What became of Jabez and Zillah Wakefield
rows.got: They emigrated with their parents and lived. JABEZ WAKEFIELD, born Bristol 1843, married in Queensland in 1863 and was buried there in 1903. ZILLAH WAKEFIELD, born Bristol 1845, married in Queensland in 1871. Both are on the General Hewitt register this archive published in July — a fact I failed to check before calling them new.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's death notices, and whether they name his family
rows.got: SEVENTEEN notices in England, Ireland and Scotland — London, Canterbury, Windsor, Oxford, Perth, Dublin, Limerick, Clonmel, Drogheda, Boyle. Four give the death as 13 MAY 1827 at Chatham, two of them within four days, which replaces Connolly's printed roll of 1898 with the contemporary press. The Kent Herald of 17 May adds “AT AN ADVANCED AGE”, and the same paper on 24 May reports that he “was interred at Chatham WITH MILITARY HONOURS” on the Saturday — 19 May 1827, the exact date of entry 1571 in Chatham's burial register. A local paper and a parish clerk, independently.

rows.what: Whether the press names Robert D'Arcy's parents
rows.got: It does not, and this is a real answer rather than a failed search. Every one of the seventeen reads “Major-General D'Arcy” and stops — no forename, no father, no seat, no county. On the very same pages other men are “only son of Mr. John Blades, of Ludgate-hill” and “fourth daughter of Charles Coleman, Esq.”; the papers of 1827 were fluent in that grammar and used none of it on him. The most promising unopened door to his parentage is now open and empty.

rows.what: What became of the three Wakefield daughters
rows.got: ELLEN WAKEFIELD was buried at BRISTOL, ST PAUL, PORTLAND SQUARE on 12 JULY 1840, AGED 5 — Bristol Archives P/St P/R/3/3. She had been baptised there on 26 October 1834, father James, mother Hannah. This archive framed her absence from the 1854 passenger list as a question about emigration; she died fourteen years before the ship, in her parents' own parish. An Eliza Wakefield appears in the same index in 1834, to be confirmed.

rows.what: Why Hannah Saniger's baptism still cannot be found
rows.got: Because only one partial index reaches it. A control — HANNAH SMITH at Berkeley 1795–1815 — returns nineteen results, and the ONLY baptism collection producing anything for Berkeley is England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975, the FamilySearch index. FindMyPast's own Gloucestershire Baptisms covers Bristol parishes and does not reach Berkeley. That index holds John Saniger's children of 1801, 1803 and 1808 and not his daughter of 1805.

rows.what: The marriage of John Saniger and Lydia
rows.got: No John Saniger marries at Berkeley between 1792 and 1804, though his children are baptised there from 1801. Lydia — whom the tree names as Hannah's mother, and who is very probably the seventy-year-old Lyddya Sinegar in Hannah's house in 1841 — is still joined to this family by nothing but a surname and a household.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's death notice, 1827
rows.got: Not reached. The newspaper archive holds 107 million pages and returns 3,886 articles for “Robert D'Arcy”, but its date filters could not be driven from a URL and narrowing needs the interface by hand. A death notice for a Major-General in May 1827 is exactly the kind of thing that names a family, and it remains the most promising unopened door to his parentage.

rows.what: Samuel Sneyd alive, and his wife's birthplace
rows.got: HO107/2004 f.138 p.13: SAMUEL SNEYD, 72, GROCER, of WELL STREET, born MADELEY, STAFFORDSHIRE; ELIZABETH his wife, 71, born OSWESTRY, SHROPSHIRE; JAMES their son, 33, engraver. Every element of the tree's claim and of this archive's 1861 identification, confirmed by one page — and it settles the unreadable “Staly Cladwin” of 1861 as OSWESTRY.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Shropshire Baptisms, Oswestry St Oswald's
rows.what: Elizabeth Oliver's baptism
rows.got: Born 17 MAY 1782, baptised 19 May, father DAVID OLIVER, mother MARY — Shropshire Archives P214/A/2/1 p.18. The tree says 7 May 1787: one digit out in the day and one in the year, and both censuses put her nearer 1780. She is the only Elizabeth Oliver baptised at Oswestry in the window the censuses point to.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Cheshire, Diocese of Chester, control-tested
rows.what: The Audlem marriage of 22 October 1809
rows.got: Not there. Audlem is indexed twice — parish marriages AND bishop's transcripts — and a control for SMITH marrying there 1804–1814 returns twenty entries. No Sneyd marries at Audlem in that window, and widening to every Sneyd record at Audlem of any date returns thirty-six results, every one a civil registration after 1837. Not one Sneyd is in Audlem's parish registers.

rows.what: James Wakefield's own baptism
rows.got: Baptised at STROUD 6 April 1806, father RICHARD WAKEFIELD, mother ELIZABETH WEBB — matching the birthplace the 1851 census gives him. It also explains the two-year-old MATILDA WEBB living in his house at Drivers Fields in 1841: his mother was a Webb.

rows.what: The marriage of Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward
rows.got: PORTSEA ST MARY, 21 JUNE 1779. The archive has carried this marriage on a family tree since it began, with nothing behind it. Their son Joseph was baptised in the same church nine months later, on 19 March 1780.

rows.what: Whether Joseph D'Arcy had brothers and sisters at Portsea
rows.got: He did not, and this is now a real null. John Smith at Portsea returns St Mary baptisms continuously for 1770, 1771, 1772, 1774, 1775, 1779, 1782, 1785, 1786, 1788, 1789, 1790, 1791 and 1792 — where FreeREG holds twenty-two months. Searching that window for every D'Arcy spelling returns Joseph and nobody else. Robert and Jean baptised one child at this parish; children born while the regiment was elsewhere are a separate question.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Berkeley St Mary the Virgin, after 1677
rows.what: The five Saniger generations this archive called untestable
rows.got: All testable, and all confirmed. Thomas Saniger baptised 23 August 1744, father Thomas — the tree's exact day. Thomas married CATHERINE COTTON at Berkeley 10 April 1769, a name never held here. John baptised 18 May 1769, father Thomas — the tree gives his birth as 15 May. Thomas buried 24 January 1819 aged 75; John buried 16 January 1825 aged 55. And John's children appear at Berkeley in 1801, 1803 and 1808, with the tree putting Hannah's birth in July 1805 exactly between them.

rows.what: Hannah Saniger's own baptism
rows.got: Not in the index, and this is a gap rather than an absence. Her father's other children are there — William 1801, John 1803, Thomas 1808 — so the register was being kept and he was using it. FamilySearch's transcription of Berkeley is not complete, and the original book is what will settle her.

rows.what: Where Hannah Saniger was born
rows.got: BERKELEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE. The 1851 census at Drivers Fields, St Paul, Bristol — the same house as the 1841 one — states her birth town and county outright, and they are the ones the family tree gave at the start. The archive's entire “not born in Gloucestershire” thesis rested on a single yes/no tick in 1841 and is wrong. The same page gives James Wakefield's birthplace as STROUD and adds two children nobody here knew of, Jabez and Zillah.

rows.what: The marriage of James Wakefield and Hannah Saniger
rows.got: Bristol, 17 OCTOBER 1831. The first English record of this marriage, and the first English record of any kind to give Hannah the surname Saniger — which until today rested entirely on five Queensland death registrations written a world away and decades later.

rows.what: Whether Berkeley's register can be searched after 1677
rows.got: It can, and with parents named. Saniger baptisms at Berkeley run Jos 1792, Ann 1798, Jno 1803, Jno and Edwd 1804, Edward 1805, Thos 1808, Victoria 1817, Eliza and Hesther 1819, Daniel 1821 — and Daniel's entry gives his father as Edward Saniger and his mother as Kitura. The five untestable Saniger generations were behind a subscription, not behind a gap in the record.

rows.what: Sanigers on the Somerset side of the Avon
rows.got: WILLIAM SANIGER married MILLE SMITH at Bedminster St John the Baptist on 29 January 1815, by banns, both of Bedminster; witnesses Wm Smith and Benjn John Room. Bishop's transcripts, Somerset Archives D/D/RR 39-40A. Real, interesting, and — now that Hannah turns out to be a Berkeley woman — not connected to this family by anything.

rows.what: Sanigers at Chew Magna
rows.got: None, in any spelling. The control passes: the same query with “berkeley” returns 252 and Chew Magna itself is covered — a Smith search there returns Somerset Burials and Somerset Baptisms. So the zero is real. Together with the 1851 census this closes the Chew Magna hypothesis, which was mine and which was wrong.

rows.what: Whether the Sanigers were at Chew Magna before Bristol
rows.got: They were. ELIZABETH SANIGAR, 45, born Somerset, is enumerated at BATTLES LANE, CHEW MAGNA in 1841 — in the house of Thomas Veale, SPADE MAKER, which is exactly the trade Collinson said the parish still had in 1791 (“a few edge-tools and stockings”). She is the same woman who appears at Oxford Road, Bristol in 1851 as a widow of 60. A Bristol clerk writing “Chew Magna” in 1851 was not mishearing anything.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — record details for all twelve RG 4 pieces
rows.what: Whether the Bristol chapel registers can actually be read online
rows.got: No. Every one of the twelve comes back DIGITISED: FALSE. RG 4 is filmed and published through commercial partners rather than free on TNA's own site. This archive said the opposite the same morning and the overclaim is filed as an error.

rows.what: A route to Portsea St Mary's register beyond FreeREG's two years
rows.got: None found. Portsmouth History Centre's parish register holdings are not reachable through Discovery in any usable form — searching for Portsea registers returns Admiralty pension papers and Royal Artillery brigade registers instead. The volumes exist; the catalogue route to them does not run through here. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.what: James and Hannah Wakefield, and the three daughters left behind
rows.got: Still nothing. Hannah Wakefield appears once — “Out of County”, aged 35, Bristol, 1841 — and not at all in 1851; the three Jameses of the right age are all 1841 entries. No Ellen Wakefield of the right age exists in either county. Given that FreeCEN's Bristol 1851 holding is real but unmeasured in depth, this remains an absence from a partial transcript.

rows.src: Hanley St John the Evangelist, burial register (FreeREG)
rows.what: Samuel Sneyd's burial
rows.got: Entry 2330: SAMUEL SNEYD, buried 23 SEPTEMBER 1855, aged 77, of 91 WELL ST. The tree says he died on 20 September 1856 at No 3 Well St. The street is right, the three-day interval between a death on the 20th and a burial on the 23rd is ordinary — and the year is wrong. The age of 77 puts his birth about 1778, which fits the Madeley baptism of 1781 this archive had already corrected to, and not the tree's 1769.

rows.what: Whether Samuel Sneyd died in 1855 or 1856
rows.got: 1855. Every Samuel Sneyd death registered anywhere in England and Wales between March 1854 and December 1858 was searched: there is EXACTLY ONE, September quarter 1855, Stoke upon Trent, volume 6b page 75. And his widow is there too — Elizabeth Sneyd, December quarter 1861, Stoke, 6b 66, confirming the tree's 1 December 1861 to the quarter.

rows.src: Collinson, History and Antiquities of the County of Somerset (1791)
rows.what: What Chew Magna was, and whether it holds Sanigers
rows.got: “A large and populous parish … six miles south-west from Bristol … one hundred and seventy houses, and eight hundred and thirty inhabitants” — and, crucially, “in former days this was a borough, a market, and a LARGE CLOTHING TOWN”. Cloth is the trade that runs through every Saniger this archive has found. No Sanigers in Collinson himself, which means nothing: he copies gentry monuments, and a journeyman smith's family would not be in them. Two figures on /chew-magna were corrected against him.

rows.what: The marriage of Samuel Sneyd and Elizabeth Oliver at Audlem, 22 October 1809
rows.got: Untestable. John Smith across the WHOLE OF CHESHIRE for 1800–1820 returns TWO entries, one at Whitegate and one at Wrenbury. It is the emptiest county holding this archive has measured, and Audlem is not in it at all. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.what: Elizabeth Margaret Oliver's baptism at Oswestry, 7 May 1787
rows.got: Untestable. Smith across Shropshire 1783–1792 returns 167 entries — Shrewsbury 70, Hodnet 15, Ludlow 10 — and NONE at Oswestry. The town is not transcribed. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.src: FreeREG — Gloucestershire, control test on the city of Bristol
rows.what: Whether Bristol's parish registers can be searched at all for 1800–1820
rows.got: They cannot. William and Mary Smith across Gloucestershire for 1800–1820 return 289 entries from 75 parishes, and exactly ONE is inside Bristol — a single entry at Stapleton, on the city's edge. St Paul, St Philip and Jacob, St James, Clifton, Bedminster, Temple, St Mary Redcliffe: none of them appears at any size. Every Bristol search this archive has ever run has been searching a city that is not in the index. The emptiness belonged to the index, not to the family.

rows.what: Where the Sanigers of Bristol came from
rows.got: A Saniger household at OXFORD ROAD, St Philip and Jacob — the parish next to St Paul, where the Wakefields lived. William Saniger, 27, journeyman smith, born SOMERSET, CHEW MAGNA; his wife Caroline, born Fishponds; and his mother ELIZABETH SANIGER, widow, 60, born SOMERSET, CHEW MAGNA. A Somerset parish, a neighbouring street, the right generation and the right trade — the first answer that meets every constraint the 1841 census imposes.

rows.src: FreeREG — Somerset, control test on Chew Magna
rows.what: Whether Chew Magna can be searched for Sanigers at all
rows.got: It cannot. Three forenames of Smith across Somerset 1795–1815 return 943 entries from over a hundred parishes, and exactly TWO of them are Chew Magna — against a hundred at Walcot and sixty-nine at Bath, in a parish of some 1,800 people. The transcript is a fragment, so the absence of Sanigers there is not evidence of anything. The only Somerset Saniger in the window is a marriage at Walcot, Edmund Liddall and Rachel Saniger, 8 June 1819.

rows.what: The three Wakefield daughters who did not sail in 1854
rows.got: Eliza, Ellen and Martha Wakefield, born Bristol 1832–1836, are not identifiable in the 1851 census, and neither is their father. FreeCEN does hold 1851 Bristol — a control on William Smith returns twelve Bristol entries for that year — but the depth of that holding is unmeasured, so this is an absence from a partial transcript rather than a finding. No Ellen Wakefield of the right age appears in either county.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — the whole catalogue, not one collection
rows.what: Everything filed under the name Saniger, in any archive
rows.got: Seventy-one records across Kew, Gloucestershire, Berkeley Castle, Bristol, Birmingham and Wiltshire. Among them the estate deeds D2957/41 that follow Edward Saniger from CLOTHIER in 1692 to GENT in 1709; a fine naming Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife in 1731; and — searching the same catalogue under Sanigear and Sanigar — two wills and a defamation suit that nobody here had ever looked for.

rows.src: Birmingham Archives MS 3549, against the Berkeley Castle Muniments
rows.what: Whether Saniger and Swanhanger are the same place
rows.got: They are, and one document proves it. The deed of 11 April 1377 between Elias de Swonhongre and William Panyter is catalogued by Berkeley under the man's name and by Birmingham as land “in SWANHANGER, co. Glouc.”. Gloucestershire Archives then glosses it outright in D654/III/9: “Oldminsters in Swanhanger … [Saniger in Hinton]”. Saniger is a worn-down Swanhanger — the wooded slope where the swans were.

rows.src: Ralph Bigland, Collections … County of Gloucester (1791), volumes I and II
rows.what: Monumental inscriptions for Saniger, Wakefield and Sneyd beyond Berkeley
rows.got: Volume II holds no Sanigers at all. Volume I holds fourteen, and six more than were extracted the first time: William Saniger of FROGPITT yeoman d. 17 Jan 1704; Edward Saniger of PEDINGTON and Mary his wife; and six neighbouring households styled “of Saniger” — Hallix, Smyth, Hyett, Pick, Bishop — none of whom is called Saniger. Twenty miles off at Minchinhampton, a second family under the -gear spelling. And in the Berkeley burial list, a William Wakefield buried 1732 aged 32.

rows.what: Which Bristol chapel registers could hold a birth about 1805–1815
rows.got: Thirty-six Bristol registers, not the five this archive's errand list had assumed. Twelve of them are births or baptisms covering 1805–1815 and the other twenty-four can be struck off without being opened. Nearly all are catalogued under SOMERSET rather than Gloucestershire, which bears directly on the 1841 census tick that says Hannah was not born in Gloucestershire.

rows.what: Samuel Sneyd's household at Hanley
rows.got: The 1861 census at WELL ST, HANLEY — “Grocers Shop” — holds James Sneyd, engraver, his wife, three children, and his MOTHER: Elizabeth Sneyd, widow, aged 82, born Shropshire. The tree says Samuel Sneyd, a grocer of Hanley, died at No 3 Well Street in 1856 leaving a widow Elizabeth Margaret Oliver of Oswestry, Shropshire, who died on 1 December 1861 — eight months after the enumerator called. Five agreements; one age eight years out.

rows.what: Whether 1841 or 1851 could be searched at all
rows.got: They cannot. John Smith, born Staffordshire 1800–1805, returns thirty-one people and every single one is 1861. FreeCEN's Staffordshire holding is 1861 and nothing else, so Samuel Sneyd — who died in 1856 — was never findable, however hard he was looked for. A null that says nothing about the family and everything about the index.

rows.src: FreeREG — Portsea St Mary, Hampshire, control test
rows.what: How much of the register stands behind Joseph D'Arcy's 1780 baptism
rows.got: Twenty-two months of it. Five common surnames across Hampshire 1778–1783 return forty-six Portsea entries: all baptisms, twenty in 1780, twenty-five in 1781, one in 1782, and NONE in 1778, 1779 or 1783. A separate control — John Smith across 1770–1800 — returns not one Portsea entry at all. The earliest English record of this family survives because it falls inside a two-year transcript, and the absence of Joseph's brothers and sisters proves nothing whatever.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's commissions, printed at the time rather than in Connolly's book
rows.got: Issue 16755, 19 July 1813, Office of Ordnance: “Brevet Colonel Robert D'Arcy to be Colonel, vice Evelegh.” One line, but it is the first primary notice of his career this archive holds, and it replaces a nineteenth-century printed roll with the Gazette that roll was compiled from.

rows.what: Smyth of Nibley's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.got: Not found in any scanned copy reachable from here; archive.org's search returns nothing under that title and the catalogue probes came back empty. The muster would name every able-bodied man in the Berkeley hundred by tithing, with trade — the single best source for Sanigers before the parish register helps. Recorded as not-yet-reached rather than not-there.

rows.src: The Berkeley Castle Muniments, via TNA Discovery
rows.what: How far back the place-name Saniger goes
rows.got: To the thirteenth century, and it settles the direction of the naming. Nine deeds name people “of Saniger” between about 1272 and 1473 — Robert Gamel, Martin Waleys, Geoffrey Nel, Philip son of Richard Couthulf, John Smyth, Richard de Egton, Walter Hevyner, Richard Webbe. NOT ONE OF THEM IS CALLED SANIGER. The place exists for two hundred years before anyone takes the name off it, and BCM/A/1/30/2 says plainly “Geoffrey Nel of Saniger IN THE PARISH OF BERKELEY”.

rows.src: Ralph Bigland, Collections relative to the County of Gloucester (1791)
rows.what: Berkeley parish — the monumental inscriptions and the freeholders
rows.got: Bigland states it outright: “SANIGER, LONG HELD BY AN OLD FAMILY OF THE SAME NAME.” And he copied the stones — Esther wife of Edward Sanger of Saniger, Gent., died 13 June 1693; Edward Saniger of Saniger, Gent., buried 3 December 1739 aged 48; Susanna his relict, 1744, aged 58; Jane his daughter, 1750, aged 24. Edward Saniger stands as the freeholder for Hinton tithing at the 1776 election. This is the post-1677 Berkeley material the parish transcript does not have, and an antiquary copied it in 1791.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — Berkeley manorial court rolls
rows.what: Where a landholding family appears when the parish register does not hold it
rows.got: They survive in quantity: Ham manor 1515–1577, Alkington 1565–1603, Canonbury 1282–1463, and — the relevant one, since Saniger lies in Hinton tithing — HINTON MANOR, GCR/231 and 258, 1523–1528. Court rolls name tenants, which is exactly how a family that holds land and rarely appears in a register is found.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — Wakefield of Bristol, Sneyd of Madeley, D'Arcy wills in Kent
rows.what: The other three British lines, through the same catalogue
rows.got: Nothing usable. 232 Wakefield-and-Bristol hits and not one is this family; no Sneyd deed for Madeley at all; and no D'Arcy will for Kent between 1820 and 1860. The catalogue that gave up a hamlet and a Welsh will has nothing for these three.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — the name Saniger in Gloucestershire records
rows.what: Any deed, will or suit naming a Saniger at Berkeley
rows.got: THE NAME IS A PLACE. Nine catalogue entries put it beyond doubt: “Deeds of Panthurst Farm, SANIGER, BERKELEY” (1716–1814); “Edward Saniger OF SANIGER, Berkeley, clothier” (1692) and “gent” (1709 and 1716); “lands in Saniger and Hamfallow, Berkeley” (1671/2); and, earliest of all, “John Saniger of Berkeley, YEOMAN” in a release of 2 November 1601. The surname is toponymic, taken from a hamlet in Berkeley parish, and the family is documented holding land there for two centuries before this archive's story begins.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — PROB 11 for the Welsh and Gloucestershire lines
rows.what: Wills for John Maddock Jones of Ruabon and for any Saniger
rows.got: PROB 11/1991/312 — the will of JOHN MADDOCK JONES OF RUABON, DENBIGHSHIRE, proved 24 January 1844. That is the man who married Robert D'Arcy's daughter in 1806, and his will would name his wife and children — a branch this archive has never had. Also PROB 11/1825/326, the will of Elizabeth Saniger, widow, of Thornbury, 1833; and at Shropshire Archives SRO 2847/7/173, a 1829 deed naming “John Maddock Jones of Penybryn esq”, the exact address on the marriage entry.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy in a printed establishment list rather than a nineteenth-century roll
rows.got: He is there, among the Second Lieutenants and Practitioner Engineers of the Corps of Engineers, beside Charles Holloway, Thomas Whelpdale, James Fiddes and Robert Beatson — two years after the commission of 17 January 1776 that Connolly gives him. And in a separate half-pay section of the same volume, a FRANCIS D'ARCY: independent support for this archive's decision to treat Francis D'Arcey of Galway, of the 39th and 45th Foot, as a different man.

rows.what: The 1806 Ruabon marriage, and the Cork and Limerick registers
rows.got: Both behind Cloudflare. That is four free British and Irish databases shut to this archive in one day — irishgenealogy.ie, NSW BDM, newspapers.library.wales and, earlier, CWGC. Each is open to a person with a browser and closed to an automated one.

rows.what: A marriage notice for a general's daughter married by licence
rows.got: The 1806 volumes are held in the Internet Archive's lending collection and their full text is not public. The Google-digitised public-domain runs do not cover that year in a form this archive could reach.

rows.src: FreeCEN — the 1851 census, every Saniger spelling in Bristol
rows.what: The Sinegar households again, in the year that records relationships and exact birthplaces
rows.got: THE BEST LEAD THIS ARCHIVE HAS. Thomas Sinegar, head, 42, labourer, of 7 Oxford Road, St Philip and Jacob Out — BORN AT BERKLEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE. His wife Martha, 42, a cordwainer, born at BERKLEY too. Of 28 Saniger-variant people in Bristol in 1851 they are the only two from Berkeley, and “Berkley” is the exact unusual spelling the family tree uses for Hannah Saniger's birthplace.

rows.src: FreeCEN — Sanigers still in the Vale, 1841
rows.what: Whether the family had wholly left Berkeley by the census years
rows.got: They had not. Samuel Saniger, 50, a shoemaker, and his son Samuel, 15, a butcher, are at Berkeley in 1841, with fifteen more of the name at Cam. The family is demonstrably in the parish through the nineteenth century — and FreeREG's Berkeley transcript stops in 1677, which is the coverage gap in its sharpest possible form.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — RG 4, the Non-Parochial Registers
rows.what: Which Bristol nonconformist register would hold a baptism of about 1805
rows.got: Named at last. The National Archives holds 36 RG 4 registers for Bristol, and FIVE of them cover 1805: RG 4/2697 (Broad Mead, Baptist, 1787–1817), RG 4/1830 (Lewins Mead, Presbyterian, 1718–1840), RG 4/388 (Bridge Street, Congregational, 1714–1837), RG 4/913 (Ebenezer Chapel King Street, Wesleyan, 1793–1819) and RG 4/1792 (Castle Green, Independent, 1784–1816). Only the Moravian register is transcribed in FreeREG. “Write to Bristol” is now five named documents.

rows.src: FreeCEN — the other Bristol Sanigers of 1841
rows.what: Whether any of the 29 is kin to Hannah
rows.got: One household is worth naming. At St Philip and St Jacob, a mile from Drivers Fields: THOMAS SINEGAR, 30, a BREWER, with Martha 31 and children James 11, LYDIA 9, Thomas 7 and Martha 2. A Saniger of the right generation, in the right city, who named a daughter Lydia. But he is entered as born in Gloucestershire and Hannah is not, and the 1841 census records no relationships. Candidate kin, and nothing more.

rows.what: John Maddock Jones, Esq., of Penybryn in Ruabon, who married Robert D'Arcy's daughter in 1806
rows.got: Not there. Denbighshire is well covered — a control returns more than 500 Smiths for 1780–1830 — and holds no John Maddock Jones at all. A Welsh gentry family joined to this one by marriage, and the transcribed registers of his own county do not have him.

rows.src: FreeREG — every William Sneyd in Staffordshire, 1735–1760
rows.what: Where William the weaver was baptised, since it is not Madeley
rows.got: There are exactly TWO William Sneyd records in the whole county for those twenty-five years, and both are Madeley: the baptism of 12 September 1742 and the burial of 29 September 1744. His baptism is not in Staffordshire's transcribed registers under any parish — not Wolstanton, not Betley, not Whitmore, not Keele.

rows.what: The diocesan second copy, which often survives where a parish book fails
rows.got: FreeREG holds none. Madeley's 78 records are 72 “Other Transcript” and 6 “Parish Register”; Staffordshire as a whole has only seven Bishop's Transcript records and not one is Madeley's. The Lichfield diocesan transcripts exist — they are simply not here. That is a named errand, not a null.

rows.src: The London Gazette — Joseph, Constantine and George Pitt D'Arcy
rows.what: Whether the other D'Arcy men were gazetted
rows.got: No Joseph D'Arcy between 1795 and 1850 — the six apparent hits are Joseph Darby and Joseph Dyas. No “Pitt D'Arcy” at all, and no D'Arcy tied to the 39th Regiment. Worth a caveat: an apostrophe in a name is exactly what nineteenth-century OCR loses, so a silent absence here is weaker evidence than the ten positive hits for Robert.

rows.src: irishgenealogy.ie — Cork and Limerick church records
rows.what: The Creech–Atkinson marriage at Carrigaline in 1853, and the Atkinson and Mulcahy lines
rows.got: Cloudflare bot verification, which this archive will not attempt to defeat. This is the third such block today and by far the most costly: it is free, it needs no login, it covers Cork and Limerick, and this archive has THREE Irish lines and has never searched an Irish record.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's career, from the government's own notices rather than a printed roll
rows.got: Ten notices name him between 1793 and 1819, each citable by issue and page. The one read in full: 19 July 1813, issue 16755, page 1431 — “Brevet Colonel Robert D'Arcy to be Colonel, vice Evelegh”, in an Office of Ordnance list of Royal Engineers promotions. The archive has cited Connolly's Roll for this career since it was built; the Gazette is the source Connolly was compiled from.

rows.what: Who Hiram and Aaron Wakefield married four months apart in 1861
rows.got: Margaret Birch's own death registration, 1898/B/30356, names her parents as JOHN BIRCH and ANNIE REEVES — so the two brothers married two daughters of one household. Nine of their children are traceable in the same index: four to Hiram and Margaret, five to Aaron and Elizabeth Ann.

rows.src: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
rows.what: The whole D'Arcy side, who were New South Welshmen and not Queenslanders
rows.got: Cloudflare bot verification, which this archive will not attempt to defeat. It is the single largest untouched index for this family: George Pitt D'Arcy died at Parramatta in 1849, George Lindsay was born there in 1829, and Charlotte crossed as an infant. Queensland's equivalent index gave this archive sixty registrations and five spellings of Saniger. A person with a browser can run it in ten minutes.

rows.src: Museums of History NSW — a blocked entry corrected
rows.what: Whether NSW State Archives is still unreachable
rows.got: It is not. This archive recorded NSW State Archives as “migrated to mhnsw.au, old URLs dead”. mhnsw.au is live and the State Archives catalogue is at search.records.nsw.gov.au, a Primo instance. Its API needs a session so it could not be queried here, but the institution is no longer between houses and the entry was out of date.

rows.what: Newspaper coverage of the voyage the family arrived on
rows.got: Trove's search will not render in this environment — a limitation already recorded in the method notes. The arrival date was confirmed independently from other sources, and the Moreton Bay Courier's shipping column for 23 December 1854 was read directly by rendition: it lists arrivals from 19 to 22 December and does not reach back to the 16th. The issue that would carry it has not been located.

rows.src: FreeREG — Hampshire and Kent, every D'Arcy
rows.what: The other eight children the tree gives Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward
rows.got: They are not there. Hampshire holds exactly one D'Arcy record in sixty years — Joseph's baptism of 1780 — and Kent holds thirteen, of which six are this family. Of ten children the tree claims, the registers of the two counties they are supposed to have lived in yield two. The Corps moved them: a son was christened at Bridgetown in Barbados in 1786, and wherever else the Board of Ordnance sent them is where the rest will be.

rows.src: FreeREG — Somerset parishes south of the Avon
rows.what: Bedminster, Long Ashton, Temple, St Mary Redcliffe and Brislington — the Bristol parishes that lay in Somerset
rows.got: Bedminster and Long Ashton ARE transcribed — a control search returns Hannah Smiths in both — and neither holds a Hannah Saniger. Temple, St Mary Redcliffe and Brislington return nothing at all and appear not to be transcribed. So the Somerset-side hypothesis survives only in the parishes nobody can search.

rows.src: Queensland BDM — the three eldest Wakefield daughters
rows.what: Eliza (b.1832), Ellen (1834) and Martha (1836), who are not on the passenger list
rows.got: No trace of any of them in Queensland, in deaths or marriages, under Wakefield or as a mother's maiden name. Twenty-two, twenty and eighteen when the General Hewitt sailed, they did not go and they do not appear to have followed. The family split at the quayside and three adult daughters stayed in England.

rows.what: The generation above James Wakefield, named on his 1857 Queensland death registration
rows.got: One candidate in the whole county: Richard Wakefield, baptised Chedworth 21 December 1770. Chedworth is in the Cotswolds, forty miles from Bristol, and nothing connects him to this family but a name and a plausible date. Recorded as a candidate and nothing more.

rows.what: Any Wakefield or Saniger of this family in the fraction of Bristol that is transcribed
rows.got: One Wakefield baptism only — Louisa, 25 November 1832, Countess of Huntingdon's Chapel, Lodge Street — and her father is James CUBIT Wakefield of St Augustine's parish, with a wife Mary. Not this family. No Saniger appears in any Bristol register at all. The transcribed fraction of Bristol has now been exhausted.

rows.src: Queensland assisted immigration index — every other family in this archive
rows.what: Sneyd, Atkinson, Atwell, Murdoch, Matson, Creech, Keeling and Blum arrivals
rows.got: Only the Wakefields came assisted. Sneyd returns nothing — correctly, since Samuel Charles arrived with the 4th (King's Own) in 1832. Paul Cole Atkinson and Jane Creech, who emigrated in 1862, are not in it; nor Eliza Keeling, nor John Blum, nor any Murdoch of the right age. The index covers assisted passages only, so the finding is that this family's other lines PAID — and the Wakefields, a mason's family of eight, took the free passage.

rows.src: FreeREG — Staffordshire, all 551 Sneyd records, reconstituted
rows.what: The Sneyd households of the Potteries, assembled rather than searched
rows.got: THE CHAIN CLOSES. William Sneyd, WEAVER — the man who married Mary Blackbourne at Madeley on 27 March 1769 — baptises thirteen children there between July 1769 and December 1794, and the 1779 entry names the mother MARY. Their SAMUEL is baptised 4 June 1781. The tree puts Samuel in 1769; the register puts him in 1781, and 1769 is the year his eldest brother William was baptised, three months after the wedding.

rows.src: FreeREG — Wiltshire, Monmouthshire, Herefordshire, Worcestershire, Shropshire, Oxfordshire
rows.what: Hannah Saniger, born about 1805, in the counties around Bristol
rows.got: Nothing. One Hannah SENGAR buried at Chaddesley Corbett in 1801, and she is a burial. Control-tested: both county groups return more than 500 Smiths for the same twenty years, and Wiltshire alone holds 358 Saniger-variant records around Salisbury and the Knoyles. Eight counties have now been searched for this woman and she is in none of them.

rows.src: FreeREG — Chatham St Mary the Virgin, Kent
rows.what: The parish Robert D'Arcy served in for decades and died in, never searched
rows.got: Seven D'Arcy records, and they are the best material this archive has ever had on the line. Robert D'Arcy buried 19 May 1827, AGE 76. Jane D'Arcy — Jean Ward — buried 21 March 1823, AGE 66. Constantine D'Arcy buried 9 May 1805, entered as “Lt in the Royal Engineers”. Margarett Maria Isabella D'Arcy married by licence in 1806, witnessed by her brother Joseph. And Charlotte, daughter of “George Pitt D'Arcy, Bt: Major 39th Foot”, born 29 April 1825 and baptised eight days before the England sailed.

rows.src: FreeREG — Hanley St John the Evangelist, Staffordshire
rows.what: The parish the tree names as Samuel Charles Sneyd's birthplace, never searched before today
rows.got: FOUND. Samuel Sneyd, born 13 March 1811, baptised 28 April 1811 — father Samuel, mother Elizabeth, abode Hanley. The tree names exactly those parents. A sister, Mary, follows in 1814 with the father's occupation recorded: SERVANT. Every previous search had gone to Madeley because that is where the disproved Keele graft pointed.

rows.src: FreeREG — Madeley All Saints, the 1769 marriage
rows.what: William Sneyd and Mary Blackbourne, whom the tree names as Samuel's parents
rows.got: Found, and it had been in the results list all along. Madeley All Saints, 27 March 1769, entry 68: William SNEYD, WEAVER, and Mary BLACKBOURNE, witnessed by Robert Sneyd and John Kidd. This archive reported the line unevidenced this morning without following it up.

rows.what: How and when the Wakefields reached Australia, and whether the passenger register gives Hannah's native place
