rows.got: FOUND, with the register scan. The ship GENERAL HEWITT, Brisbane, 16 December 1854, 394 souls. James Wakefield 48, a MASON — matching the 1841 census's “Mason Journeyman” — with Hannah 48, Jabez 11, Zillah 8 and Ephraim 5; Hiram 16 a plumber and Aaron 14 entered separately among the single men, both native place BRISTOL; and Marion Wakefield 14, a domestic, among the single women, also Bristol. Marion is Miriam. The emigration is now dated to the day.

rows.src: QSA digital image DR38490 — the passenger register itself
rows.what: Whether the register gives Hannah Wakefield's own county
rows.got: It does not. Her county is a ditto mark under her husband's “Gloucester”, which is the household head's county and not a statement about her. The register plainly distinguishes the two — it enters her three eldest children as Bristol on the same day — so the ditto cannot be read as her birthplace. Hannah's origin remains the open question.

rows.src: FreeREG — every Saniger record in Gloucestershire, opened individually
rows.what: All 556 records read one by one and reconstituted into households, rather than searched by name
rows.got: 81 households assembled from 196 baptisms naming a father. Not one has a mother called Lydia; not one is a John and Lydia; there is a single Hannah baptised in the whole county, at Stinchcombe in 1730; and only three households bear children between 1795 and 1815. Hannah is not in Gloucestershire — which the 1841 census had already said by entering her as born out of the county.

rows.src: FreeBMD — deaths, Lydia Saniger and every spelling, 1841–1875
rows.what: Lyddya Sinegar of the 1841 census, who should have died in England
rows.got: Not there. A deliberately loose phonetic search — loose enough to return SCHONSWAR and SMOOKER — finds no Lydia Saniger, Sanigar or Sinegar death in Bristol in those thirty-four years. The nearest are an infant Lydia Ann Sanigear at Islington in 1847 and an unnamed SANIGAR at Thornbury in 1851. Either she died under a married surname, or under a spelling the index does not reach.

rows.what: Hannah Wakefield's exact birthplace, which 1841 does not give
rows.got: Not applicable, and worth recording as such: the family had emigrated. James Wakefield died at Brisbane in July 1857, so by 1861 there was nobody in England to enumerate. The plan to get Hannah's birthplace from a later English census was sound and the family had left before it could work. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.src: FreeREG — the marriage of John Saniger and Lydia Jones
rows.what: About 1795–1804, wherever Hannah was born
rows.got: Cannot be attempted usefully. Hannah was born outside Gloucestershire and the archive does not know where, so there is no parish to search; and if the marriage was at Berkeley the transcript ends in 1677 regardless. This one needs Hannah's birthplace first, and that now depends on a certificate.

rows.src: FreeREG — Madeley All Saints, the two baptisms the tree asks for
rows.what: William Sneyd bapt. 1746 and Samuel Sneyd bapt. 1769, both said by the tree to be at Madeley
rows.got: Neither exists. Madeley holds Samuel 1745, Joseph 1746, John 1748, Simeon 1751 and no William; and its only Samuel is baptised 1781. The parish is transcribed continuously — 110 Sneyd records from 1699 — so both are real absences. This archive had been using a 1742 William instead, four years off the tree's date, and that child may be the one buried in 1744.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — deaths, searched by MOTHER's name
rows.what: Every Queensland death registration whose mother is recorded as a Saniger
rows.got: THE ANSWER. Five of Hannah's children died in Queensland and every registration names her: Ephraim 1868 “Anna Sanniger”, Aaron 1896 “Hannah Sanegar”, Zillah 1900 “Hannah Saniger”, Hiram 1905 “Hannah Sanigar”, Miriam 1909 “Hannah Saniger”. Five clerks, forty-one years, four spellings — and the father given as James Wakefield on all five.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — Hannah Wakefield's own death
rows.what: Her parents, from her own registration
rows.got: Registration 1873/C/603, died 4 July 1873 — matching the tree to the day. Her father is entered as “John JENNIGER”. The tree says John Saniger. A capital S read as a J is one of the commonest misreadings in nineteenth-century clerking, and the forename and the rest of the surname agree exactly. Her mother is not given.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — James Wakefield's death
rows.what: The father of the family, died Brisbane 8 July 1857
rows.got: Registration 1857/B/135, and it names HIS father: RICHARD WAKEFIELD. A generation the archive did not have, and the first Wakefield above James anywhere.

rows.what: Miriam Wakefield's marriage, and her siblings'
rows.got: Miriam Wakefield married WILLIAM HARTLEY SNEYD on 15 November 1859 at Brisbane, registration 1859/B/255 — the marriage that joins the Wakefields to the Sneyds, and she was nineteen, not twenty-one as this archive had said. Her brothers Hiram and Aaron married Margaret and Elizabeth Ann BIRCH four months apart in 1861; Jabez married Margaret Fraser in 1863; Zillah married John Ludwig Frederick in 1871.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — Lydia Saniger
rows.what: Whether Lyddya Sinegar of the 1841 census followed her family to Queensland
rows.got: No Lydia Saniger death is registered in Queensland under any spelling. She was seventy in 1841; the family did not emigrate until after 1849. She stayed, and died, in England.

rows.what: Any trace of Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward at Portsea, where the tree says they married on 21 June 1779
rows.got: FOUND, and it is the first record of Robert D'Arcy in an English parish register this archive has ever had. Joseph D'ARCY, baptised Portsea St Mary 19 March 1780 — father ROBERT, mother JEAN. Nine months after the marriage the tree asserts, at the same church. It is the only D'Arcy record in the whole county.

rows.what: The real Sneyd line under the disproved Keele graft
rows.got: 110 Sneyd records at Madeley All Saints. The 1742 baptism that killed the Keele claim reads: William Sneyd, 12 September 1742, father William Sneyd. And two years later: “William, son of William SNEYD”, buried 29 September 1744. If that is the same child — and in one small parish it is the obvious reading — the archive's Sneyd line is anchored to a boy who died at two.

rows.what: The generation above Francis Murdoch of St Quivox
rows.got: 128 Murdoch records in Ayrshire, across Galston, Tarbolton, Ayr, Kirkoswald, Loudoun, Dailly, Beith and Dunlop — and St Quivox is not among the parishes with data. The county is thinly covered (202 Smiths for the whole of the eighteenth century) and the one parish this archive needs is not in it.

rows.what: Jean Ward, born South Leith 1754
rows.got: Midlothian's holding is Edinburgh, Canongate, Restalrig and Dalry. South Leith is not transcribed. Not a null result — the parish is simply not there.

rows.what: Richard Atkinson and Anne, and anything else in the county
rows.got: Zero records for the entire county. A control search for SMITH across the whole of the eighteenth century returns nothing at all. FreeREG lists County Limerick in its search form and holds no data for it.

rows.what: Surname Wakefield, whole county; then the household page itself
rows.got: THE FIND. HO107/374, enumeration district 13, page 10, dwelling 1615, Drivers Fields, civil parish of St Paul, Bristol: James Wakefield 35 a mason journeyman, Hannah 35, Hiram 4, Aaron 1, Miriam 1 — and Lyddya SINEGAR, 70, Independent. The tree records Hannah's mother as Lydia and her brother Jabez born at “Drivers Field”; neither was copied from this record, which nobody in the family had read.

rows.what: The same household ten years on, for the relationships and exact birthplaces 1841 does not give
rows.got: 221 Gloucestershire Wakefields are transcribed for 1851 and 31 of them in Bristol, but not this family. Nationally only 36% of the 1851 pieces are online and the piece covering Drivers Fields is not among them. A coverage gap, not an absence — and the record that would turn the Lyddya Sinegar inference into a fact.

rows.what: Whether the tree's “Berkley, Gloucester” is really Berkley in Somerset, which would explain Hannah being born out of county
rows.got: It is not. Berkley Somerset is transcribed in full — 7,967 records, 1545–1903 — and the family there is spelled SINGER in every one of 58 entries, with no Hannah baptised near 1805. A clean answer to a good question.

rows.what: Where the Vale of Berkeley Sanigers went
rows.got: 97 across Gloucestershire, 29 of them in Bristol, spelled SINEGAR, SUNIGAR, SENGEIR, SANGER and SINGER. The family did leave the Vale, and Bristol is where a good part of it went.

rows.what: Every register FreeREG holds for Bristol, checked before searching rather than after
rows.got: Four registers and 1,551 records for a city of 120,000: Countess of Huntingdon's Chapel (81, 1820–1837), Methodist Bishopston (98, 1891–1915), Moravian Maudlin Street (1,016, 1755–1865) and Temple of Holy Cross (356, 1834–1849). St Paul, Bristol — where the tree says Miriam Wakefield was baptised — is not among them. The Wakefield–Saniger join cannot be tested here, and any “not found” would have been a lie.

rows.src: FreeREG — coverage tool, the Vale of Berkeley
rows.what: Dursley, Cam, Thornbury, Stinchcombe, Coaley, Slimbridge, Uley, North Nibley, Wotton-under-Edge
rows.got: Dursley St James runs 1577–1951 with 30,784 records and Cam St George 1568–1939 with 17,150. Both cover the whole of the archive's Saniger chain. The /berkeley page had implied those generations were untestable because Berkeley stops in 1677; they were testable all along, three miles away.

rows.what: Fuzzy surname search, all record types, whole county
rows.got: 494 records. Cam 184, Dursley 156, Thornbury 55, Berkeley 18. Three baptisms match the tree's dates almost exactly: Thomas at Dursley 17 Mar 1711/12, William at Dursley 6 Nov 1743, William at Dursley 27 Sep 1770.

rows.src: FreeREG — the three Dursley baptisms, opened
rows.what: The full transcription of each, to read the fathers
rows.got: The chain fails. Thomas 1711/12 is the son of ABRAHAM; William 1743 the son of JOHN; William 1770 the son of SAMUEL. Three men who happen to be baptised in the right parish in the right years, and no two of them are father and son. The date-match was a coincidence.

rows.what: The generation the tree puts at 1805
rows.got: None. Not a coverage gap: Dursley runs to 1951 and Cam to 1939, so the window is well covered. The tree's 1805 Saniger does not exist in Gloucestershire.

rows.what: Where the family goes after the chain is supposed to leave Berkeley
rows.got: 139 records, continuous through the whole century, centred on Cam (67), Dursley (28) and Thornbury (17). The family never leaves the Vale — and in 139 records it never once marries a Wakefield.

rows.src: FreeREG — Hannah Saniger, GLS, SOM and WIL, 1780–1880
rows.what: The one Saniger the archive actually needs: Miriam Wakefield's mother
rows.got: 35 fuzzy matches and not one of them in Gloucestershire. All are Somerset and Wiltshire SINGER or SANGER — different families the phonetic match swept up. Hannah Saniger is not in the Gloucestershire registers.

rows.what: Miriam Wakefield, born Bristol 11 April 1840
rows.got: FOUND. Birth registered June quarter 1840, Bristol district, volume 11, page 183 — the only Miriam Wakefield registered anywhere in England between 1839 and 1843. A birth on 11 April falls in the June quarter exactly as it should. Her GRO certificate names her mother with her maiden surname, which would test “Saniger” directly.

rows.what: A Wakefield–Saniger marriage, every spelling, 1837–1870
rows.got: None. The earliest Saniger or Sanigar marriage registered in the Bristol district is John Sanigar in the March quarter of 1846 — six years after Miriam was born. Control-tested: the same harness returns 21,248 Wakefield marriages for 1838–1842, so the search works and the absence is real. James Wakefield and Hannah Saniger did not marry in Bristol after civil registration began on 1 July 1837.

rows.what: Every spelling of D'Arcy and Sneyd against Brisbane and Queensland papers, 1840–1950; obituaries, funeral notices, insolvency reports, memorial notices
rows.got: Lindesay D'Arcy's 1936 obituary, confirming five details of a eulogy delivered 74 years later and restoring one the family had lost — that he served in France. George Pitt D'Arcy's 1849 obituary and the verdict “gout which had flown to the head”. The 1926 insolvency and the 1927 fraudulent-preference action against the bank. Arthur Sneyd's memorial notices and “Ruby”. Vivian Claude Sneyd at Gallipoli.

rows.what: “Sneyd” and “D'Arcy” across every series; then item-level fetches through the JSON API
rows.got: Forty-one items under Sneyd. The find of the day: coronial file ITM2736504 (DR103140), an inquest nobody in the family knew existed. Also the 1873 insolvency of William Hartley Sneyd, Arthur's 1916 intestacy, four wills, two police staff files and nine land dealings.

rows.what: Every Sneyd, D'Arcy, Blum, Wakefield and Murdoch death registration, 1856–1996
rows.got: Sixty registrations, eighteen of them published. Queensland death registrations name the deceased's parents, which is why this one free index carries more proved relationships than every other source on this page combined.

rows.src: National Archives of Australia — RecordSearch, series B2455
rows.what: Three AIF service dossiers, read page by page at native resolution
rows.got: Arthur Hartley Sneyd 5050 (30 pp.), Vivian Claude Sneyd 1696 (21 pp.), Ernest Vivian William Sneyd 3891 (92 pp.). Arthur's corrected his trade from clerk to typist and his burial from “France” to no known grave.

rows.what: The Red Cross Wounded and Missing Enquiry Bureau file for 5050 Sneyd
rows.got: Twenty-three pages, six witness statements, six different answers. A friend still searching thirteen months later from a lecture room at New College, Oxford.

rows.what: Honours and awards recommendation files for Sneyd
rows.got: The Bar to Vivian Claude Sneyd's Military Medal, in full: Westhoek, 4 October 1917, signed by Lieut-Col A. Graham Butler and endorsed “Awarded”.

rows.what: D'Arcy wills in PROB 11; WO 97 discharge papers; ADM 101 surgeons' journals; Ordnance series
rows.got: PROB 11/1728/64 — Robert D'Arcy's own will, proved 4 July 1827, digitised and unordered. ADM 101/26/1, the surgeon's journal of the convict ship England, which names Major George Pitt D'Arcy four times and closes a 23-year loop on how he died.

rows.what: Full-text sweep of the colony's civil establishment lists for every family surname
rows.got: Thirty-seven years of Sneyds on the Queensland payroll. William Hartley Sneyd, Fount-room Overseer at the Government Printing Office on £225, in the public service from 1 February 1862 — matching his widow's sworn “about 12 years” to the year.

rows.what: Every spelling of Saniger, 1600–1677, plus a county-wide fuzzy sweep
rows.got: Forty-four Sainger entries at Berkeley and 238 across the county. One candidate baptism, 24 May 1655, giving a father the archive never had — Edward Sainger of Wanswell. And the unexpected result: the surname's centre is Dursley and Cam, not Berkeley.

rows.src: Connolly, Roll of Officers of the Corps of Royal Engineers
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy and Constantine D'Arcy
rows.got: Entry 203 — Robert's whole career, 2nd Lt 1776 to Major-General 1819, C.B., died Chatham 13 May 1827. Entry 335 — Constantine, died Chatham 6 May 1805. Neither entry records a parent, which is itself the finding.

rows.what: Murdoch of St Quivox, Ayrshire
rows.got: A generation documented. Also the reason the DNA points here: this is a quarter of the tested descendant and the archive has half its ancestor slots empty.

rows.what: One living descendant's result, against the tree's own prediction
rows.got: Agreement, not contradiction: British Isles 80.1% measured against 93.4% predicted. And the test that matters — cutting both grafts moves the prediction by 0.39 of a percentage point.

rows.src: National Archives of Australia — B2455, D'Arcy
rows.what: Lindesay Atkinson D'Arcy's AIF dossier, under every spelling of the name
rows.got: Nothing. The method was then control-tested by running the same query for his brother-in-law Arthur Sneyd, which returned his dossier at once — so the absence is real and not a bad search. The archive had previously claimed a fourteen-page dossier “is known to exist”; that claim was withdrawn.

rows.what: The will of the 4th Earl of Holderness
rows.got: No PCC will that can be found. This was the single best hope of testing whether the Earl acknowledged a natural son, and it is not there to test.

rows.what: An obituary or death notice for Major-General Robert D'Arcy, C.B.
rows.got: Empty. A Companion of the Bath and a colonel of Engineers died at Chatham and the magazine of record did not notice. That silence is part of the argument on /hornby.

rows.what: A baptism for Robert D'Arcy, c.1750–1758
rows.got: Nothing, under any spelling. Combined with Connolly recording no parentage and the Gentleman's Magazine recording no death, the parentage question is not disputed — it is unknown.

rows.src: WO 149 — Royal Military Academy Woolwich cadet registers
rows.what: A cadet of the early 1770s
rows.got: The wrong record set entirely: WO 149 begins in 1790 and is held at Sandhurst. The archive had recommended it without checking its date range, and said so. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.what: The citation for Vivian Claude Sneyd's first Military Medal
rows.got: The Gazette records the award but does not name him in a citation. The Bar was found instead, at the AWM.

rows.what: A service record for Samuel Charles Sneyd, Governor of Brisbane Gaol
rows.got: Searched twice. He appears exactly once in the whole QSA catalogue and it is not a service record. A man who ran a colonial gaol for over a decade has left no staff file that survives.

rows.what: Five generations of the Saniger chain, 1679 to 1805
rows.got: Not a null result and must not be reported as one: the Berkeley transcript stops in 1677. The records may well exist in the parish books; they are absent from the transcription, which is a different thing.

rows.what: Where Arthur Hartley Sneyd is commemorated
rows.got: Bot-blocked, twice. A free two-minute search that a person can run and this archive cannot.

rows.what: Mounted Police and convict-era records for Samuel Charles Sneyd
rows.got: The catalogue migrated to mhnsw.au and the old URLs are dead. Between houses.

rows.what: General searching beyond the two files reached by direct URL
rows.got: Mid-migration. Two documents were reached by constructing S3 URLs directly; the search itself would not answer.

rows.what: Newspaper coverage of William Hartley Sneyd's insolvency
rows.got: The QSA file proves the insolvency exists. Trove's search interface would not surface the notice, repeatedly. The file itself is not digitised.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: The whole county, for the Saniger surname — all seventeen spellings this archive holds, plus every surname in Gloucestershire ending -gar, -gear, -ger, -gor and -gre
rows.got: Eleven men in four spellings — Saniger (5), Sanyger (3), Syniger (2), Sainger (1). One, John Sainger, weaver, is living in the hamlet of Saniger in Hinton parish, Berkeley. SANYGER and SYNIGER were not among the seventeen spellings held here.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: Thirteen spellings of the surname that returned nothing: Sanigar, Sanigear, Sanegar, Saneger, Sannigar, Sanniger, Sannegar, Sanger, Sinegar, Sinnegar, Siniger, Sinigar, Sinager, Sineger
rows.got: All genuinely absent, control-tested: the same interface returned 676 men for Dursley and 42 for Halmore. Every form ending -GAR is missing from 1608, which dates the -GAR spellings as later than the -GER ones rather than older.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: SWANHANGER, as both a surname and a place name
rows.got: Nothing under either. The tithing is written 'Saniger [in Hinton parish, Berkeley]' by 1608, so the older form had already gone out of written use — consistent with the deeds, which carry Swanhanger to 1741 only as an antiquarian spelling.

rows.what: The scanned text of the 1980 reprint (menarmourforglou0000smyt)
rows.got: A lending item: the full text returns HTTP 401 and the search-inside endpoints are retired. Reading it would need an Archive.org account and a loan. The 1902 edition's transcript at coaley.net answered instead.

rows.what: A register lookup: the marriage of John Saniger and Lydia at Berkeley St Mary the Virgin, c.1795–1800, and confirmation of Hannah Sanigor's baptism of 18 August 1804
rows.got: Answered in one day and declined: the office does not offer a research service of any kind. It named two routes instead — the Gloucestershire Family History Society, whose volunteers do lookups, and Ancestry, which holds the filmed county registers with marriages and banns to 1938. The record is not unreachable; this door is.

rows.src: Smyth, A Description of the Hundred of Berkeley (c.1639, printed 1885)
rows.what: The full text of volume 3 of The Berkeley Manuscripts, for Saniger, Sanyger, Swanhanger, Swonhungre and every OCR-plausible variant
rows.got: Fourteen occurrences of Saniger, three of Sanyger, eight of Swonhungre. Smyth heads the hamlet “Swonhunger; corruptly called Saniger”, describes it as thirteen dwelling houses in the manor of Hame, and gives its owner in 1639 with four generations of male ancestors — John, son of John, son of Maurice, son of Robert, son of William. Also Robert Saniger buying a manor in 1541 and John Saniger of Saniger acting as a trustee. Control: Berkeley 1,497 hits, Hinton 53, Nibley 73 in the same file.

rows.what: All spellings of the surname across every repository Discovery indexes: Saniger, Sanigar, Sanyger, Sainger, Syniger, Swanhanger, Swonhunger
rows.got: Seventy-one records under Saniger, forty-four under Sanigar, three under Swanhanger, two under Swonhunger, none under Syniger. Six that were new here — a fine of 1731 naming Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife, a consistory-court defamation of 1768, the 1617 trustee deed Smyth describes without dating, John Saniger yeoman in 1601, a coroner's inquest on Elizabeth Saniger aged 3 of Cam in 1856, and an inquisition post mortem of 1626 — plus twelve Berkeley Castle deeds naming people “of Saniger” between before 1291 and 1473. Sanyger and Sainger returned only Devon, Norfolk, Sussex and Reading records belonging to other families.

rows.what: All 26 Sneyd war dead, and the casualty record for Arthur Hartley Sneyd
rows.got: Casualty 1451888 confirms the Villers-Bretonneux MEMORIAL — not the military cemetery of the same name, which holds a different Sneyd, Rex, 49th Bn, died 14 June 1918. Service number 5050, 9th Bn A.I.F., died 20 August 1916 aged 22, son of Arthur and Martha Sneyd of James St., Wooloowin, born at Rockhampton. Nothing here was new; everything here was already published, and is now sourced to the authority instead of inferred.

rows.what: The baptism of LYDIA JONES at Wotton-under-Edge, about 1770, to William Jones and Sarah
rows.got: Not a null — the parish is not transcribed. Lydia Jones, Gloucestershire baptisms 1760–1785: nil. But JONES of any forename at WOTTON-UNDER-EDGE, all record types, 1740–1800: also nil — nought entries for the commonest surname in England across sixty years. The same search across the county returns 164 Jones baptisms in a narrower window, so the engine works and the county is covered. Wotton-under-Edge appears in FreeREG's place list and has effectively no eighteenth-century transcription behind it, which is the coverage-tool-versus-search disagreement this archive has already recorded once.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Registration Service Index (with the Gloucestershire FHS)
rows.what: All deaths registered under the stem SANIG across Gloucestershire, 1837–1899, sweeping in five-year steps
rows.got: Twenty-four deaths, each with the registrar's own register and entry number rather than a GRO quarterly reference — including LYDIA SANIGAR, 1851, register 3, entry 265, who this archive has wanted since it began. Coverage was checked before searching: Thornbury/Berkeley deaths complete 1837–1948, Dursley 1837–1937, Wotton-under-Edge 1837–1937. A free index nobody here had used.

rows.src: Staffordshire Name Indexes — Diocese of Lichfield and Coventry Wills, 1550–1810
rows.what: SNEYD, all 36 records, and SNEYD of MADELEY
rows.got: Thirty-six Sneyd wills, ten of them at Keele — and the tenth is RICHARD SNEYD, LABOURER, of Keele, 1772, in the same parish and the same court as four Ralph Sneyds, esquires and gentlemen. Sneyd of MADELEY returns nothing; control is the same search without a place, which returns all thirty-six.

rows.src: Staffordshire Name Indexes — the site as a whole
rows.what: The Madeley burials of the 1740s, and Lichfield bishop's transcripts generally
rows.got: Structurally out of scope. The site indexes twenty-six Staffordshire collections — wills, apprentices, asylums, gaol calendars, tithe awards, workhouse admissions — and no parish registers or bishop's transcripts of any kind. It cannot answer errand 19 and never could.

rows.src: Smyth, The Berkeley Manuscripts, volumes 1 and 3 (1883–85)
rows.what: Every occurrence of Swonhunger, Swanhunger, Saniger and Sanyger across both volumes — the twenty-five page references in Smyth's own index
rows.got: Forty-four distinct passages. A pedigree of the hamlet's owners from Thomas de Stone (died 1315–16) to John Swonhungre, who died without issue in 1401–2 leaving two sisters; the place in the free-warren charters of Henry II to Edward I; a grant of a yard land at Swonhunger dated 1189; Nigell of Swonhunger temp. Richard I; John de Swonhongre, esquire, in Lord Berkeley's retinue in 1326; and the hinge for the later branch — William Swonhunger, Crown lessee under Henry VIII, father of Robert, father of John.

rows.src: The National Archives — PROB 11 digitised wills
rows.what: Whether PROB 11/1825/326 (Elizabeth Saniger), PROB 11/1728/64 (Major-General Robert D'Arcy) and PROB 11/1991/312 can be downloaded
rows.got: All three are digitised and open, and all three read “£3.50 - sign in to get this free”. The charge is waived for any registered user and registration is free, so these are not paid records — they are free records behind a free account. This archive creates no accounts, so they stay on the errand queue, but at nil cost rather than £10.50.

rows.src: The National Archives — Discovery, the other surnames
rows.what: SINEGAR, SANIGRE, COTTON of Berkeley, WAKEFIELD with Saniger, and D'Arcy with the Royal Engineers at Chatham
rows.got: COTTON of Berkeley gives the first document from Catherine Cotton's side of the family: PROB 11/1056/294, the will of Benjamin Cotton, cordwainer of Berkeley, proved 16 September 1779, eleven months after her burial in the same parish. D'ARCY with Chatham returns Robert D'Arcy's own will and twenty plans of the Chatham Lines from 1804 to 1821 — MR 1/553/3, and the MFQ 1/1280 and MFQ 1/1315 series — drawn across the years this archive says he was chief engineer there.

rows.what: SINEGAR and SANIGRE as surnames
rows.got: Sanigre: nothing at all. Sinegar: three records and not one is a person — a Bisley police station called Sinegar House in 1950 and 1984, and an unrelated Sussex account of 1705. Both spellings are productive in the Bristol and Berkeley registers and neither has left a catalogued document anywhere.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Registration Service Index — births and marriages
rows.what: All births and all marriages under the stem SANIG, 1837–1893, swept in five-year steps
rows.got: Twenty-seven births and ten marriages, each with a local register and entry number, and the marriage index giving both partners — Ford, White, Stephens, Stockwell, Watts, Dore, Sinnett, Young, Powell. Read against the twenty-four deaths already taken, seven names appear as both a birth and a death at intervals of one to nine years. The birth form also accepts a MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME as a search term, which makes a guessed maiden name testable.

rows.src: Whitworth Porter, History of the Corps of Royal Engineers (1889)
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy, and the Corps' own account of the stations and sieges he served at
rows.got: Five mentions, indexed by Porter as one man: Lieutenant Robert D'Arcy at the siege of Fort St Philip's, Minorca, 1781; “Robert D'Arcy, Barbados” in a station list, confirming from the Corps what this archive had inferred from two christenings; Lieutenant-Colonel R. D'Arcy as COMMANDING ENGINEER of the Copenhagen expedition of 1807; and as Commanding Royal Engineer at Walcheren in 1809, where — “an old man beyond sixty” — he refused to write a report for a wounded superior he claimed to outrank, was put under arrest, and apologised only after the court-martial was arranged. Free, out of copyright, and never opened here before.

rows.what: All SNEYD deaths in Staffordshire, 1837 onward — a free local index nobody here had used
rows.got: 276 Sneyd deaths, each with AN AGE AT DEATH, a sub-district and a local register reference — none of which the GRO quarterly index gives. Errand 10's target is there and independently confirms what this archive already had: SNEYD, Samuel, aged 77, 1855, HANLEY sub-district, registers at Stoke-on-Trent, reference HAN/011/023, matching the Hanley burial of 23 September 1855 aged 77 of 91 Well Street. The certificate can now be ordered against the local reference.

rows.what: Whether Bristol and Somerset have local registrars' indexes like Gloucestershire's and Staffordshire's
rows.got: They do not. The project lists Gloucestershire and Staffordshire — both used today, both productive — but neither Bristol nor Somerset has a dedicated local index. For the Bristol Wakefields and the Chew Magna Smiths there is no equivalent of the reference that found Lydia Sanigar.

rows.src: Internet Archive — Rudder, A New History of Gloucestershire (1779)
rows.what: Saniger, Swanhanger and the Berkeley hundred parishes in the full text
rows.got: The text download returns HTTP 503 and an error page. Control: the file contains nought occurrences of BERKELEY, DURSLEY and HINTON, which is impossible for this book — so the download failed rather than the book being silent. Recorded as unreachable, not as a null.

rows.src: Internet Archive — Collections for a History of Staffordshire (William Salt Society)
rows.what: Sneyd of Keele pedigrees, and any Madeley branch, in two volumes of the series
rows.got: Nothing genealogical in the two volumes reachable: one has no Sneyd at all, the other has exactly one — in the society's own list of subscribers, “Sneyd, Rev. Walter, Keele Hall, Newcastle”, a living member in the 1880s. The series runs to dozens of volumes and the pedigree material is in ones not identified here. Control: Staffordshire itself appears 90 and 49 times, so the files are sound.

rows.src: The National Archives — research guides and Discovery API
rows.what: Which series holds a Board of Ordnance engineer's commission of 1776; the piece-level arrangement of IR 26 for 1876; and the right series for a British death at Le Havre in 1843
rows.got: WO 54/240, Engineers 1755–1780, is the only Board of Ordnance commission book covering the 1770s, with WO 47/87–88 as the minutes that would date the appointment. IR 26 runs to 1903, not 1857, and the 1876 C–D will registers are IR 26/2941–2947, chosen by the folio number in IR 27/396/3. RG 35/8–13 is the France run for foreign death returns, gated by the digitised index RG 43/4. None of the three is name-indexed free.

rows.what: Whether the Death Duty registers stop in 1857, which would make the Catherine D'Arcy errand impossible
rows.got: They do not. 1857 is where the MICROFILMING stops — the registers themselves run 1796–1903 and the 1876 pieces are open, catalogued and held at Kew, merely unfilmed and offline. A widely repeated access boundary mistaken for a records boundary, and the errand survives it.

rows.src: Calendars of Inquisitions Post Mortem, volumes 5–8 (Edward II – Edward III)
rows.what: SWONHUNGER in every spelling, and THOMAS DE STONE, whose two daughters carry Smyth's pedigree
rows.got: Neither family is in four volumes of the printed Calendars. Controlled twice: Gloucester appears 230–334 times per volume and Berkeley 15–17, so the county is covered; and a fragment search on “hungr”/“hunge”, tolerant of the volumes' poor OCR, returns Gravenhunger, Clehungre and Trewonhan — names of exactly that shape — so the search reaches them. The explanation is structural: a royal inquisition was taken only for a tenant-in-chief, and the Swonhungers held of Lord Berkeley, not of the king. The absence is what the record type predicts.

rows.what: Swonhunger, Swanhunger, Swonhungre and Saniger across its published series
rows.got: A CAPTCHA on every search URL, in curl and in a real browser alike. This archive does not complete CAPTCHAs, so the site is unreachable from here. It publishes the Victoria County History and the calendars of Close, Fine and Patent Rolls, all of which would be worth a human's ten minutes.
